derivations.search:
**Setting.** Choose a descent direction $p$ at $\theta$, with $g_0^\top p<0$. Let $\varphi(\alpha)=J(\theta+\alpha p)$, $\alpha>0$, and $0<c_1<c_2<1$.

#### 1 · Differentiate the one-dimensional restriction
The chain rule gives $\varphi'(\alpha)=\nabla J(\theta+\alpha p)^\top p$. In particular $\varphi'(0)=g_0^\top p<0$.

#### 2 · Write both weak Wolfe conditions
Sufficient decrease (Armijo) requires
$$\varphi(\alpha)\le\varphi(0)+c_1\alpha\varphi'(0).$$
The curvature condition requires
$$\varphi'(\alpha)\ge c_2\varphi'(0).$$
Because the initial derivative is negative and $c_2<1$, the second condition requires the slope to become less negative. An arbitrarily tiny step may pass Armijo but fail curvature.

#### 3 · Express the secant pair’s inner product
Let $s=\alpha p$ and $y=\nabla J(\theta+\alpha p)-g_0$. Then
$$y^\top s=\alpha[\nabla J(\theta+\alpha p)^\top p-g_0^\top p]
=\alpha[\varphi'(\alpha)-\varphi'(0)].$$

#### 4 · Apply the curvature inequality
$$y^\top s\ge\alpha(c_2-1)\varphi'(0)>0.$$
The strict positivity follows because $\alpha>0$, $c_2-1<0$, and $\varphi'(0)<0$. This is the condition needed in the preceding BFGS proof.

#### 5 · Relate strong Wolfe
Strong Wolfe uses $|\varphi'(\alpha)|\le c_2|\varphi'(0)|$. This implies $\varphi'(\alpha)\ge-c_2|\varphi'(0)|=c_2\varphi'(0)$, so it also supplies the lower bound above. These arguments assume all evaluations describe the same differentiable objective; fresh dropout masks or different mini-batches can undermine that interpretation.

title: Diagnosing optimization versus generalization
summary: Interpret symptoms before changing the model, optimizer, or regularization.
search:
First identify which part of the learning process is failing The guides distinguish at least three possibilities: the model cannot represent what matters, the optimization procedure is not reaching a useful parameter region, or the fitted function fails to generalize. Similar-looking final scores can arise for different reasons. For example, high errors on both training and validation can reflect underfitting, difficult optimization, inadequate inputs, or too much regularization. A tiny training error with weak validation is instead consistent with overfitting. More dropout is not a universal answer, and a more powerful optimizer is not a universal answer either. Read the training symptoms Observation from the guides Possible explanation What the explanation suggests checking Loss explodes immediately Excessive rate or numerical instability Initialization, finite values, gradient norms, output/loss pairing Very slow improvement Small rate, poor conditioning, weak gradients Feature scale, derivative flow, rate and schedule Strong oscillation Large steps or a narrow valley Momentum, conditioning, step-size control Training improves, validation worsens Generalization failure Capacity, penalties, valid augmentation, stopping time AdaGrad stalls late Large permanent accumulator Effective coordinate rates and recent-gradient alternatives BFGS unstable with mini-batches Noisy curvature differences Objective consistency and deterministic/full-batch suitability These are hypotheses, not diagnoses guaranteed by a curve. Inspect the underlying computation before treating the pattern as proof. Monitor the update, not only the loss The optimization PDF suggests monitoring J_t,\qquad \lVert g_t\rVert,\qquad\lVert\Delta\theta_t\rVert,\qquad
\frac{\lVert\Delta\theta_t\rVert}{\lVert\theta_t\rVert+\epsilon}. The last ratio asks whether an update is small or large relative to the existing parameter scale. A tiny gradient is not automatically harmless; it might be a symptom of saturation. A large gradient is not automatically a useful learning signal; it might be an instability. Interpret each quantity with the activation and objective scales. The official TensorBoard tutorial already demonstrates graph, data, and training visualizations. Use it to inspect a real run rather than reconstruct another dashboard inside these notes. Step by step Derive global-norm clipping as a projection Setting. A finite gradient vector g\in\mathbb R^d and radius c>0 . Seek the vector closest to g inside the Euclidean ball: \min_u\frac12\|u-g\|^2\quad\text{subject to }\|u\|\le c. 1 · Check the feasible unconstrained optimum The derivative of \tfrac12\|u-g\|^2 is u-g . Its unconstrained minimum is u=g . If \|g\|\le c , this is feasible and already solves the constrained problem. In particular g=0 stays zero; no division is required. 2 · Handle a gradient outside the ball If \|g\|>c , the optimum lies on its boundary. Use the Lagrangian \mathcal L(u,\lambda)=\tfrac12\|u-g\|^2+\tfrac\lambda2(\|u\|^2-c^2),\qquad\lambda\ge0. Stationarity gives u-g+\lambda u=0 , hence u=g/(1+\lambda) . 3 · Enforce the boundary radius \|u\|=\frac{\|g\|}{1+\lambda}=c\quad\Rightarrow\quad
1+\lambda=\frac{\|g\|}{c}. Substituting yields u=cg/\|g\| . 4 · Combine the two cases \tilde g=\begin{cases}g&\|g\|\le c,\\ cg/\|g\|&\|g\|>c.\end{cases} For nonzero g , this is g\min(1,c/\|g\|) . Norm clipping preserves direction on the clipped branch; clipping each coordinate independently does not generally do so. 5 · Distinguish gradient and update bounds For basic SGD, \Delta\theta=-\eta\tilde g implies \|\Delta\theta\|\le\eta c . With momentum or adaptive state, the update also depends on previous history. Bounding the fresh gradient alone does not establish the same bound on the final parameter displacement. A deeper network that fails where a simpler one succeeds should first be checked for these issues. Check a small forward calculation, verify that each output has the intended meaning, and confirm that gradients connect the loss to the relevant parameters. The running forward/backward example provides a compact numerical reference for what a correct chain should look like. Step by step Derive a directional finite-difference gradient check Setting. Hold the data and all randomness fixed. Let v be a unit direction and assume J is sufficiently smooth along \theta+tv . A directional check compares g^\top v with a scalar finite difference. 1 · Write both Taylor expansions J(\theta+hv)=J(\theta)+h g^\top v+\frac{h^2}{2}v^\top Hv+O(h^3), J(\theta-hv)=J(\theta)-h g^\top v+\frac{h^2}{2}v^\top Hv+O(h^3). 2 · Subtract to cancel the even-order terms The constant and quadratic terms cancel, leaving J(\theta+hv)-J(\theta-hv)=2h g^\top v+O(h^3). Divide by 2h : \frac{J(\theta+hv)-J(\theta-hv)}{2h}=g^\top v+O(h^2). The centered check has second-order truncation error. 3 · Explain why a smaller step is not always better Finite-precision evaluations subtract nearly equal numbers. A rough roundoff contribution scales like \epsilon_{\mathrm{machine}}|J|/h , while truncation scales like h^2 . Making h arbitrarily small trades one error for the other; use a range of sensible steps and double precision for a numerical check. 4 · Respect nonsmooth and stochastic computations At a ReLU kink, the classical derivative may not exist, and centered differences need not match a chosen subgradient. Different stochastic masks evaluate different functions, invalidating the subtraction. Avoid kink crossings and freeze randomness before interpreting a discrepancy as a backpropagation error. 5 · Use checks as evidence, not a proof A passing directional check supports correctness along that direction at that parameter point. Multiple independent directions, analytically tractable cases, and shape tests provide stronger coverage. They do not prove every possible input and branch is correct. Expanded derivation Chapter source · PDF p. 23 Link to this calculation ↗ Regularization effects can accumulate Strong weight decay, high dropout, aggressive augmentation, and early stopping all restrict the learned solution in different ways. Their combined effect can produce underfitting. The regularization PDF explicitly warns against adding more constraints when both training and validation remain weak. Augmentation also needs a credible target-preservation assumption. A model trained on corrupted labels may look difficult to optimize when the real problem is that its effective training task is inconsistent. Compare complete procedures fairly Optimizer names alone do not define experiments. Base rate, schedule, batch size, momentum, decay, and stopping criteria all affect outcomes. BFGS and CG additionally depend heavily on line search and curvature safeguards. Tune within a validation procedure and compare computation as well as validation performance. The validation set used to choose those settings is part of model selection. Repeatedly choosing settings from the test score changes the role of the test data. For temporal problems, the guides emphasize time ordering and resampling schemes that preserve the intended dependence. A practical order is to establish a correct objective and derivative path, obtain reliable training behavior, and then address the gap to unseen data. Changing many components simultaneously makes that reasoning harder, because a better result no longer reveals which change addressed the failure.

derivations.title: Derive global-norm clipping as a projection
derivations.search:
**Setting.** A finite gradient vector $g\in\mathbb R^d$ and radius $c>0$. Seek the vector closest to $g$ inside the Euclidean ball:
$$\min_u\frac12\|u-g\|^2\quad\text{subject to }\|u\|\le c.$$

#### 1 · Check the feasible unconstrained optimum
The derivative of $\tfrac12\|u-g\|^2$ is $u-g$. Its unconstrained minimum is $u=g$. If $\|g\|\le c$, this is feasible and already solves the constrained problem. In particular $g=0$ stays zero; no division is required.

#### 2 · Handle a gradient outside the ball
If $\|g\|>c$, the optimum lies on its boundary. Use the Lagrangian
$$\mathcal L(u,\lambda)=\tfrac12\|u-g\|^2+\tfrac\lambda2(\|u\|^2-c^2),\qquad\lambda\ge0.$$
Stationarity gives $u-g+\lambda u=0$, hence $u=g/(1+\lambda)$.

#### 3 · Enforce the boundary radius
$$\|u\|=\frac{\|g\|}{1+\lambda}=c\quad\Rightarrow\quad
1+\lambda=\frac{\|g\|}{c}.$$
Substituting yields $u=cg/\|g\|$.

#### 4 · Combine the two cases
$$\tilde g=\begin{cases}g&\|g\|\le c,\\ cg/\|g\|&\|g\|>c.\end{cases}$$
For nonzero $g$, this is $g\min(1,c/\|g\|)$. Norm clipping preserves direction on the clipped branch; clipping each coordinate independently does not generally do so.

#### 5 · Distinguish gradient and update bounds
For basic SGD, $\Delta\theta=-\eta\tilde g$ implies $\|\Delta\theta\|\le\eta c$. With momentum or adaptive state, the update also depends on previous history. Bounding the fresh gradient alone does not establish the same bound on the final parameter displacement.

derivations.title: Derive a directional finite-difference gradient check
derivations.search:
**Setting.** Hold the data and all randomness fixed. Let $v$ be a unit direction and assume $J$ is sufficiently smooth along $\theta+tv$. A directional check compares $g^\top v$ with a scalar finite difference.

#### 1 · Write both Taylor expansions
$$J(\theta+hv)=J(\theta)+h g^\top v+\frac{h^2}{2}v^\top Hv+O(h^3),$$
$$J(\theta-hv)=J(\theta)-h g^\top v+\frac{h^2}{2}v^\top Hv+O(h^3).$$

#### 2 · Subtract to cancel the even-order terms
The constant and quadratic terms cancel, leaving
$$J(\theta+hv)-J(\theta-hv)=2h g^\top v+O(h^3).$$
Divide by $2h$:
$$\frac{J(\theta+hv)-J(\theta-hv)}{2h}=g^\top v+O(h^2).$$
The centered check has second-order truncation error.

#### 3 · Explain why a smaller step is not always better
Finite-precision evaluations subtract nearly equal numbers. A rough roundoff contribution scales like $\epsilon_{\rm machine}|J|/h$, while truncation scales like $h^2$. Making $h$ arbitrarily small trades one error for the other; use a range of sensible steps and double precision for a numerical check.

#### 4 · Respect nonsmooth and stochastic computations
At a ReLU kink, the classical derivative may not exist, and centered differences need not match a chosen subgradient. Different stochastic masks evaluate different functions, invalidating the subtraction. Avoid kink crossings and freeze randomness before interpreting a discrepancy as a backpropagation error.

#### 5 · Use checks as evidence, not a proof
A passing directional check supports correctness along that direction at that parameter point. Multiple independent directions, analytically tractable cases, and shape tests provide stronger coverage. They do not prove every possible input and branch is correct.

title: Generalization and the bias–variance trade-off
summary: Explain why fitting harder can hurt, and why different regularizers constrain different parts of learning.
search:
Generalization is not the same as fitting The regularization guide asks how to constrain, perturb, average, or stop a learning algorithm so that it behaves better on unseen data. Its starting observation is that flexible models can fit accidental sample structure alongside stable signal. A penalty makes this preference explicit: \hat\theta\in\mathop{\mathrm{argmin}}_\theta\left[\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n\ell_i(\theta)+\lambda\Omega(\theta)\right]. A large penalty discourages a region of parameter space; it does not prove that the retained functions are the correct ones. The statistical usefulness depends on whether the preference matches the problem. The squared-error decomposition At a fixed input x , write Y=f(x)+\epsilon . Under the usual zero-mean noise assumptions, the source gives \mathbb E_{D,\epsilon}\left[(Y-\hat f_D(x))^2\right]
=\sigma_\epsilon^2+\left(\mathbb E_D\hat f_D(x)-f(x)\right)^2+
\operatorname{Var}_D\left(\hat f_D(x)\right). The dataset D is random in this thought experiment: imagine repeatedly collecting a training set and refitting the procedure. Bias is the distance between the average fitted prediction and the true function. Variance measures how much the fitted prediction changes across those datasets. Irreducible noise is uncertainty in the outcome even if the function were known. An expanded derivation adds and subtracts \mathbb E_D\hat f_D(x) inside the squared error. The centered estimator term has expectation zero; with the stated noise assumptions, the cross terms vanish. The remaining terms are precisely noise, squared bias, and estimator variance. This is a decomposition for squared-error prediction, not an identical additive formula for every classification metric. The supplied guide’s illustrative bias–variance curve. It is a conceptual example of competing effects, not a universal shape or a rule for selecting λ without validation. Regularization · PDF p. 5 Step by step Expand prediction error into noise, bias, and variance Setting. Fix an input x . Write a new outcome as Y=f(x)+\varepsilon , where f(x)=\mathbb E[Y\mid x] , \mathbb E[\varepsilon\mid x]=0 , and \mathbb E[\varepsilon^2\mid x]=\sigma^2(x) . The training sample D is independent of this new outcome given x . Expectations over D also include any randomization used to fit the model. 1 · Insert the mean fitted prediction Let \mu(x)=\mathbb E_D[\hat f_D(x)] . Add and subtract \mu(x) : Y-\hat f_D(x)=\varepsilon+[f(x)-\mu(x)]+[\mu(x)-\hat f_D(x)]. The middle term is fixed once x and the training procedure are fixed. The final term varies with the training sample and has mean zero. 2 · Expand all six terms of the square Abbreviate b=f(x)-\mu(x) and v=\mu(x)-\hat f_D(x) . Then (\varepsilon+b+v)^2=\varepsilon^2+b^2+v^2+2\varepsilon b+2\varepsilon v+2bv. None of the cross terms may simply be dropped before checking its expectation. 3 · Evaluate the cross terms separately Because b is fixed and \mathbb E[\varepsilon]=0 , \mathbb E[\varepsilon b]=0 . Because \mathbb E_D[v]=\mu-\mathbb E_D[\hat f_D]=0 , \mathbb E_D[bv]=0 . Finally, independence of the new noise and training sample gives \mathbb E[\varepsilon v]=\mathbb E[\varepsilon]\mathbb E_D[v]=0 . 4 · Recognize the three remaining expectations \mathbb E_{D,\varepsilon}[(Y-\hat f_D(x))^2]=\sigma^2(x)+[\mu(x)-f(x)]^2+\mathbb E_D[(\hat f_D(x)-\mu(x))^2]. The last term is the variance of the fitted prediction. The squared middle term is squared bias; its sign does not matter because it is squared. 5 · State the scope of the identity This is an identity for squared error at a fixed input, assuming the stated moments exist. Integrating it over a test-input distribution gives an average-risk decomposition. It is not the same formula for zero–one classification error, and it is not valid to treat training residuals as independent new-outcome errors. Increasing regularization does not force every individual term to change monotonically in every model. derivations.title: Expand prediction error into noise, bias, and variance
derivations.search:
**Setting.** Fix an input $x$. Write a new outcome as $Y=f(x)+\varepsilon$, where $f(x)=\mathbb E[Y\mid x]$, $\mathbb E[\varepsilon\mid x]=0$, and $\mathbb E[\varepsilon^2\mid x]=\sigma^2(x)$. The training sample $D$ is independent of this new outcome given $x$. Expectations over $D$ also include any randomization used to fit the model.

#### 1 · Insert the mean fitted prediction
Let $\mu(x)=\mathbb E_D[\hat f_D(x)]$. Add and subtract $\mu(x)$:
$$Y-\hat f_D(x)=\varepsilon+[f(x)-\mu(x)]+[\mu(x)-\hat f_D(x)].$$
The middle term is fixed once $x$ and the training procedure are fixed. The final term varies with the training sample and has mean zero.

#### 2 · Expand all six terms of the square
Abbreviate $b=f(x)-\mu(x)$ and $v=\mu(x)-\hat f_D(x)$. Then
$$(\varepsilon+b+v)^2=\varepsilon^2+b^2+v^2+2\varepsilon b+2\varepsilon v+2bv.$$
None of the cross terms may simply be dropped before checking its expectation.

#### 3 · Evaluate the cross terms separately
Because $b$ is fixed and $\mathbb E[\varepsilon]=0$, $\mathbb E[\varepsilon b]=0$. Because $\mathbb E_D[v]=\mu-\mathbb E_D[\hat f_D]=0$, $\mathbb E_D[bv]=0$. Finally, independence of the new noise and training sample gives $\mathbb E[\varepsilon v]=\mathbb E[\varepsilon]\mathbb E_D[v]=0$.

#### 4 · Recognize the three remaining expectations
$$\mathbb E_{D,\varepsilon}[(Y-\hat f_D(x))^2]=\sigma^2(x)+[\mu(x)-f(x)]^2+\mathbb E_D[(\hat f_D(x)-\mu(x))^2].$$
The last term is the variance of the fitted prediction. The squared middle term is squared bias; its sign does not matter because it is squared.

#### 5 · State the scope of the identity
This is an identity for squared error at a fixed input, assuming the stated moments exist. Integrating it over a test-input distribution gives an average-risk decomposition. It is not the same formula for zero–one classification error, and it is not valid to treat training residuals as independent new-outcome errors. Increasing regularization does not force every individual term to change monotonically in every model.

derivations.title: Derive OLS and Ridge from individual coefficient derivatives
derivations.search:
**Setting.** Let $X\in\mathbb R^{n\times p}$, $\beta\in\mathbb R^p$, and $y\in\mathbb R^n$. Center columns and targets so the intercept can be handled separately. Use the **sum-loss convention**
$$J(\beta)=\frac12\sum_{i=1}^n\left(y_i-\sum_{k=1}^pX_{ik}\beta_k\right)^2+\frac\lambda2\sum_{k=1}^p\beta_k^2,\qquad\lambda\ge0.$$

#### 1 · Differentiate one residual
Define $r_i=y_i-\sum_kX_{ik}\beta_k$. Only the term with $k=j$ changes with $\beta_j$, so $\partial r_i/\partial\beta_j=-X_{ij}$. The chain rule gives
$$\frac{\partial(r_i^2/2)}{\partial\beta_j}=r_i(-X_{ij}).$$
The penalty derivative is $\partial(\lambda\sum_k\beta_k^2/2)/\partial\beta_j=\lambda\beta_j$.

#### 2 · Add the observation contributions
$$\frac{\partial J}{\partial\beta_j}=-\sum_iX_{ij}\left(y_i-\sum_kX_{ik}\beta_k\right)+\lambda\beta_j.$$
Collecting these $p$ coordinates gives
$$\nabla_\beta J=-X^\top(y-X\beta)+\lambda\beta.$$

#### 3 · Set the gradient to zero and collect coefficients
$$-X^\top y+X^\top X\beta+\lambda\beta=0,$$
$$(X^\top X+\lambda I)\beta=X^\top y.$$
If $\lambda>0$, the matrix is positive definite: for any nonzero $v$,
$$v^\top(X^\top X+\lambda I)v=\|Xv\|^2+\lambda\|v\|^2>0.$$
Thus the stationary point is the unique global minimum and
$$\hat\beta_\lambda=(X^\top X+\lambda I)^{-1}X^\top y.$$
Numerically, solve this linear system rather than explicitly forming its inverse.

#### 4 · Recover OLS and handle rank deficiency
Set $\lambda=0$. If $X$ has full column rank, $X^\top X$ is invertible and the OLS formula follows. Otherwise the normal equations still characterize minimizers, but there may be infinitely many coefficient vectors; $X^+y$ selects the minimum-Euclidean-norm solution.

#### 5 · Track normalization and the intercept
For $\|y-X\beta\|^2/(2n)+\lambda\|\beta\|^2/2$, the system is $(X^\top X+n\lambda I)\beta=X^\top y$. The same symbol $\lambda$ therefore has a different numerical scale. With an unpenalized intercept, differentiation gives $\hat b=\bar y-\bar x^\top\hat\beta$; centering is what made it disappear above.

derivations.title: Derive the spectral shrinkage factors and the constraint connection
derivations.search:
**Setting.** Use the sum-loss Ridge objective above. Take a thin SVD over the $r$ positive singular values: $X=U_rD_rV_r^\top$, with $D_r=\operatorname{diag}(d_1,\ldots,d_r)$ and $d_j>0$. Both $U_r$ and $V_r$ have orthonormal columns.

#### 1 · Express the normal equations in singular directions
Since $X^\top X=V_rD_r^2V_r^\top$ and $X^\top y=V_rD_rU_r^\top y$, write the coefficient as $\beta=V_ra+\beta_\perp$, where $V_r^\top\beta_\perp=0$. The data-fit term cannot see $\beta_\perp$, while $\lambda>0$ penalizes it, so the minimizer has $\beta_\perp=0$.

#### 2 · Solve one coordinate at a time
Premultiply the normal equations by $V_r^\top$:
$$(D_r^2+\lambda I)a=D_rU_r^\top y.$$
If $c_j=u_j^\top y$, this says $(d_j^2+\lambda)a_j=d_jc_j$. Therefore
$$a_j=\frac{d_j}{d_j^2+\lambda}c_j,\qquad
\hat\beta_\lambda=V_r\operatorname{diag}\left(\frac{d_j}{d_j^2+\lambda}\right)U_r^\top y.$$

#### 3 · Compare coefficients and fitted values with OLS
The minimum-norm OLS coordinate is $a_j^{\rm OLS}=c_j/d_j$. Their ratio is
$$\frac{a_j}{a_j^{\rm OLS}}=\frac{d_j^2}{d_j^2+\lambda}$$
when the denominator coordinate is nonzero; the same multiplier identity holds even when $c_j=0$. Multiplying by $X$ yields
$$\hat y_\lambda=U_r\operatorname{diag}\left(\frac{d_j^2}{d_j^2+\lambda}\right)U_r^\top y.$$
Small $d_j^2$ receive the strongest shrinkage. Original-feature coefficients mix singular directions, so an individual $\beta_k$ need not decrease monotonically in magnitude.

#### 4 · Check the orthogonal example
If $X^\top X=I$, all singular values are one and $\hat\beta_\lambda=\hat\beta_{\rm OLS}/(1+\lambda)$. For $(3,-2,0.5)$ and $\lambda=1$, divide each coordinate by two to get $(1.5,-1,0.25)$.

#### 5 · Connect to a constrained problem without assuming a one-to-one map
For minimizing $\|y-X\beta\|^2/2$ subject to $\|\beta\|^2\le t$, the Lagrangian is
$$\mathcal L(\beta,\nu)=\frac12\|y-X\beta\|^2+\nu(\|\beta\|^2-t),\qquad\nu\ge0.$$
Stationarity gives $X^\top(X\beta-y)+2\nu\beta=0$, the Ridge equation with $\lambda=2\nu$. Complementary slackness requires $\nu(\|\beta\|^2-t)=0$. When a constraint is inactive, several $t$ values can share the same unregularized solution. Equivalence of appropriate solutions does not imply a globally one-to-one correspondence at every endpoint.

title: LASSO, subgradients, and exact zeros

A subgradient $s$ at zero must satisfy $|u|\ge |0|+s(u-0)=su$ for **every** real $u$. For positive $u$, divide by $u$ to obtain $s\le1$. When $b>0$, $F'(b)=b-z+\lambda$. Setting it to zero gives $b=z-\lambda$. This belongs to the assumed positive branch only when $z>\lambda$.

#### 3 · Solve the negative branch
When $b<0$, $F'(b)=b-z-\lambda$. Setting it to zero gives $b=z+\lambda$, which is negative only when $z<-\lambda$.

At $b=0$, stationarity means $0\in-z+\lambda[-1,1]$. For $\lambda>0$ this is equivalent to $z/\lambda\in[-1,1]$, or $|z|\le\lambda$. The $\lambda=0$ case reduces to minimizing a quadratic, with solution $b=z$.

$$b^*=\begin{cases}z-\lambda&z>\lambda,\\0&|z|\le\lambda,\\z+\lambda&z<-\lambda,\end{cases}

For $\lambda=0.7$, the inputs $2.4$, $0.5$, and $-1.1$ produce $1.7$, $0$, and $-0.4$. At $z=\pm\lambda$, both adjacent formulas meet at zero.

A proximal-gradient step on $f(\beta)+\lambda\|\beta\|_1$ first sets $z=\beta-\eta\nabla f(\beta)$, then minimizes $\|b-z\|^2/(2\eta)+\lambda\|b\|_1$. **Setting.** Minimize $J(\beta)=\|y-X\beta\|^2/(2n)+\lambda\sum_k|\beta_k|$. Hold every coefficient except $\beta_j=b$ fixed. Assume $a_j=x_j^\top x_j/n>0$, where $x_j$ is column $j$ of $X$.

#### 1 · Separate the coefficient being updated
Define $r^{(-j)}=y-\sum_{k\ne j}x_k\beta_k$. The residual involving $b$ is $r^{(-j)}-x_jb$. Penalties for the other coefficients are constant during this update.

#### 2 · Expand the square explicitly
$$(r^{(-j)}-x_jb)^\top(r^{(-j)}-x_jb)
=r^{(-j)\top}r^{(-j)}-2b x_j^\top r^{(-j)}+b^2x_j^\top x_j.$$
Let $z_j=x_j^\top r^{(-j)}/n$. After dropping only constants independent of $b$, the objective is $a_jb^2/2-z_jb+\lambda|b|$.

#### 3 · Complete the square
$$\frac{a_j}{2}b^2-z_jb=\frac{a_j}{2}\left(b-\frac{z_j}{a_j}\right)^2-\frac{z_j^2}{2a_j}.$$
The final term is constant. Divide the objective by positive $a_j$ and apply the scalar proof with center $z_j/a_j$ and threshold $\lambda/a_j$.

#### 4 · Simplify the update
$$\beta_j\leftarrow\operatorname{soft}\left(\frac{z_j}{a_j},\frac\lambda{a_j}\right)
=\frac{\operatorname{soft}(z_j,\lambda)}{a_j}.$$
The last equality follows by pulling the positive factor $1/a_j$ through both $|\cdot|$ and the maximum. For unit empirical mean-square columns, $a_j=1$.

#### 5 · Translate to the sum-loss convention
For $\|y-X\beta\|^2/2+\lambda_{\rm sum}\|\beta\|_1$, use $x_j^\top x_j$ and $x_j^\top r^{(-j)}$ without $n$ in their definitions. Equivalent objectives require $\lambda_{\rm sum}=n\lambda$. Keeping the same numerical penalty while changing only the loss reduction changes the fitted model.

title: Elastic Net and correlated predictors
summary: Separate total penalty strength from the balance between selection and stabilization.
search:
Combine two distinct effects The guide defines Elastic Net as \hat\beta\in\mathop{\mathrm{argmin}}_\beta\left[
\frac1{2n}\lVert y-X\beta\rVert_2^2+
\lambda\left(\alpha\lVert\beta\rVert_1+
\frac{1-\alpha}{2}\lVert\beta\rVert_2^2\right)\right],\quad0\le\alpha\le1. The L1 part encourages sparse coefficients. The L2 part stabilizes weakly identified directions and makes it easier for correlated predictors to share weight. It is not simply a compromise between two names; it combines two geometrically different preferences. \lambda sets how much total regularization is applied. \alpha sets how LASSO-like the penalty is. Those are separate questions, and both belong inside model selection. Read the endpoints carefully At \alpha=1 , the L2 contribution vanishes and the stated mean-scaled LASSO objective remains. At \alpha=0 , only L2 remains. The guide says “Ridge up to parameterization conventions” because its earlier Ridge section uses a different normalization of the fitting term. The same caution applies to library APIs. The symbol called \alpha in one source can be a total strength in another library, while l1_ratio can play the role of the PDF’s mixing parameter. The practical invariant is the objective actually minimized , not the parameter name. Why correlation changes the choice The source imagines two predictors with correlation 0.95 measuring approximately the same latent signal. A possible LASSO fit is (1.8,0) ; a Ridge fit might be (1.0,0.9) ; an Elastic Net fit might be (1.15,0.75) while eliminating other weak variables. These are illustrative coefficients, not outputs derived from a fully specified dataset. Their purpose is to show different behavior: one method selects one correlated representative, one spreads weight continuously, and the combined penalty can retain a group while still removing unrelated features. The instability of selecting only one representative is especially relevant when interpretations are attached to individual coefficient identities. A stable prediction does not imply stable variable membership. A one-coordinate view In a standardized coordinate calculation, the update has the schematic structure \beta_j\leftarrow
\frac{\operatorname{soft}(z_j,\lambda\alpha)}{1+\lambda(1-\alpha)}. The numerator performs the L1 thresholding. The denominator performs additional L2 shrinkage. The exact denominator includes the coordinate’s design norm when it is not normalized as assumed here. This decomposition is an efficient way to remember what each term does. The source’s illustrative Elastic Net paths. Zeroing and continuous shrinkage coexist; the paths are examples, not a guarantee that every correlated group will be selected together. Regularization · PDF p. 12 Step by step Derive the Elastic Net update and its grouping effect Setting. Use J=\|y-X\beta\|^2/(2n)+\lambda_1\|\beta\|_1+(\lambda_2/2)\|\beta\|^2 , where \lambda_1=\lambda\alpha and \lambda_2=\lambda(1-\alpha) . Assume \lambda_1,\lambda_2\ge0 . 1 · Add the L2 contribution to the coordinate quadratic With the same r^{(-j)} , a_j=x_j^\top x_j/n , and z_j=x_j^\top r^{(-j)}/n as in LASSO, the variable part is \frac{a_j+\lambda_2}{2}b^2-z_jb+\lambda_1|b|. For a_j+\lambda_2>0 , the three-case subgradient calculation gives \beta_j\leftarrow\frac{\operatorname{soft}(z_j,\lambda_1)}{a_j+\lambda_2}. When a_j=1 , this becomes \operatorname{soft}(z_j,\lambda\alpha)/[1+\lambda(1-\alpha)] . 2 · Explain why identical predictors share weight under an L2 term Suppose x_1=x_2 and their total coefficient is s=\beta_1+\beta_2 . The prediction depends on s , not its allocation. Write \beta_1=s/2+d and \beta_2=s/2-d . Their squared penalty is \beta_1^2+\beta_2^2=(s/2+d)^2+(s/2-d)^2=s^2/2+2d^2. It is uniquely minimized at d=0 . Their L1 penalty obeys |\beta_1|+|\beta_2|\ge|s| , with equality at the equal split. Therefore a positive L2 term favors \beta_1=\beta_2=s/2 . Pure LASSO can have many allocations with the same total and L1 penalty. 3 · Quantify a local grouping statement for similar columns Let r=y-X\hat\beta . For two nonzero fitted coefficients with the same sign , stationarity gives \frac{x_j^\top r}{n}=\lambda_1\operatorname{sign}(\hat\beta_j)+\lambda_2\hat\beta_j, and the corresponding equation for k . Subtracting cancels the L1 terms: \lambda_2(\hat\beta_j-\hat\beta_k)=\frac{(x_j-x_k)^\top r}{n}. For \lambda_2>0 , Cauchy–Schwarz yields |\hat\beta_j-\hat\beta_k|\le\frac{\|x_j-x_k\|\,\|r\|}{n\lambda_2}. If both columns have norm \sqrt n and empirical inner-product correlation \rho , then \|x_j-x_k\|^2=2n(1-\rho) . The bound tightens as same-oriented columns become similar, but it assumes matching coefficient signs and is not a blanket statement about every correlated variable. For temporal data, the guide specifically calls for time-ordered validation. Selecting the penalty by repeatedly inspecting the final test performance would undermine that comparison. In its 500-observation, 200-predictor hypothetical case, the guide contrasts these regularized linear choices with a neural approach using penalties, dropout, and early stopping. The common goal is reliable unseen-data performance; the different interventions encode different assumptions about the structure to retain. title: Augmentation, invariance, and noise injection
summary: Explain what a valid transformation teaches and derive the exact noise–Ridge connection for linear regression.

Augmentation encodes a statement about the target Let T be a sampled transformation. The augmented objective is L_{\mathrm{aug}}(\theta)=\frac1n\sum_i\mathbb E_T\left[\ell(y_i,f_\theta(Tx_i))\right]. The crucial assumption is that the chosen transformation preserves the relevant target. If y(Tx)=y(x) , training on both variants encourages an invariance such as f_\theta(Tx)\approx f_\theta(x) . This is stronger and more specific than “more data is good.” A transformed example can be harmful when its original label is no longer valid. The regularization guide gives orientation-sensitive images, text, medical anatomy, and structurally constrained tabular data as settings where careless transformations can be misleading. The source visualizes augmented observations as local clouds around original points. Whether such a cloud is valid depends on the task’s target-preserving transformations. For classification-style invariance, assume the label remains valid: y(Tx)=y(x) . For segmentation or other equivariant tasks, both input and target must instead transform consistently. 1 · Start with the loss for a single transformed example For observation i , the loss is \ell(y_i,f_\theta(Tx_i)) . Since training can see different transformations of the same example, its expected contribution is the integral \mathbb E_T[\ell(y_i,f_\theta(Tx_i))]=\int\ell(y_i,f_\theta(Tx_i))q(dT). 2 · Average over the observed sample J_{\mathrm{aug}}(\theta)=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n\mathbb E_T[\ell(y_i,f_\theta(Tx_i))]. A single random transform per selected observation is a Monte Carlo estimate of this expectation. It does not make the augmented observations statistically independent new labels. 3 · Obtain a stochastic gradient under explicit assumptions Assume differentiation may pass under the integral, for example through a locally integrable dominating bound on the derivative. Then \nabla J_{\mathrm{aug}}(\theta)=\frac1n\sum_i\mathbb E_T[\nabla_\theta\ell(y_i,f_\theta(Tx_i))]. If I is a fresh uniform index and T\sim q , then \mathbb E_{I,T}[\nabla_\theta\ell(y_I,f_\theta(Tx_I))]=\nabla J_{\mathrm{aug}}(\theta) . A transformation policy learned jointly with the model requires differentiating its parameter dependence too; this argument holds q fixed. 4 · Separate encouragement from exact invariance The objective rewards low loss over sampled variations, but does not algebraically enforce f_\theta(Tx)=f_\theta(x) . For an exact finite-group construction, define \bar f(x)=|G|^{-1}\sum_{g\in G}f(gx) . Random augmentation merely encourages related behavior through optimization and finite samples. Duplicating one observation changes its weight in the objective; duplicating every observation equally leaves a mean objective unchanged. **Setting.** A transformation $T$ is drawn from a fixed distribution $q$ independently of the parameters. For classification-style invariance, assume the label remains valid: $y(Tx)=y(x)$. For segmentation or other equivariant tasks, both input and target must instead transform consistently.

#### 1 · Start with the loss for a single transformed example
For observation $i$, the loss is $\ell(y_i,f_\theta(Tx_i))$. Since training can see different transformations of the same example, its expected contribution is the integral
$$\mathbb E_T[\ell(y_i,f_\theta(Tx_i))]=\int\ell(y_i,f_\theta(Tx_i))q(dT).$$

#### 2 · Average over the observed sample
$$J_{\rm aug}(\theta)=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n\mathbb E_T[\ell(y_i,f_\theta(Tx_i))].$$
A single random transform per selected observation is a Monte Carlo estimate of this expectation. It does not make the augmented observations statistically independent new labels.

#### 3 · Obtain a stochastic gradient under explicit assumptions
Assume differentiation may pass under the integral, for example through a locally integrable dominating bound on the derivative. Then
$$\nabla J_{\rm aug}(\theta)=\frac1n\sum_i\mathbb E_T[\nabla_\theta\ell(y_i,f_\theta(Tx_i))].$$
If $I$ is a fresh uniform index and $T\sim q$, then $\mathbb E_{I,T}[\nabla_\theta\ell(y_I,f_\theta(Tx_I))]=\nabla J_{\rm aug}(\theta)$. A transformation policy learned jointly with the model requires differentiating its parameter dependence too; this argument holds $q$ fixed.

#### 4 · Separate encouragement from exact invariance
The objective rewards low loss over sampled variations, but does not algebraically enforce $f_\theta(Tx)=f_\theta(x)$. For an exact finite-group construction, define $\bar f(x)=|G|^{-1}\sum_{g\in G}f(gx)$. For any $h\in G$, the products $gh$ enumerate $G$ again, so
$$\bar f(hx)=\frac1{|G|}\sum_{g\in G}f(ghx)=\frac1{|G|}\sum_{u\in G}f(ux)=\bar f(x).$$
Exact group averaging provides invariance by construction. Random augmentation merely encourages related behavior through optimization and finite samples.

derivations.title: Expand the exact noise–L2 identity, then identify the nonlinear remainder
derivations.search:
**Setting.** Hold $X,y,\beta$ fixed. Let the $n$ noise rows $\varepsilon_i^\top$ have mean zero and covariance $\Sigma_\varepsilon$. Put them into $E$, so noisy predictions are $(X+E)\beta$. Gaussianity is not needed for the quadratic expectation; the stated first two moments suffice.

#### 1 · Expand the residual norm before taking expectations
Let $r=y-X\beta$. Then
$$\|r-E\beta\|^2=r^\top r-2r^\top E\beta+\beta^\top E^\top E\beta.$$
Since $\mathbb E[E]=0$, the middle term has expectation zero.

#### 2 · Evaluate the remaining random term row by row
$$\|E\beta\|^2=\sum_{i=1}^n(\varepsilon_i^\top\beta)^2
=\sum_i\beta^\top\varepsilon_i\varepsilon_i^\top\beta.$$
Taking expectations gives $\mathbb E\|E\beta\|^2=n\beta^\top\Sigma_\varepsilon\beta$. Therefore
$$\mathbb E\|y-(X+E)\beta\|^2=\|y-X\beta\|^2+n\beta^\top\Sigma_\varepsilon\beta.$$
For isotropic covariance $\Sigma_\varepsilon=\sigma^2I$, this is the source’s $n\sigma^2\|\beta\|^2$ penalty. For mean half-squared loss, divide every term by $2n$, giving penalty $\sigma^2\|\beta\|^2/2$.

#### 3 · See what changes for a nonlinear predictor
For one input, use loss $L(x)=\frac12[f(x)-y]^2$, residual $r=f(x)-y$, gradient $a=\nabla_xf(x)$, and Hessian $H_f$. A second-order expansion is
$$f(x+\varepsilon)-y=r+a^\top\varepsilon+\tfrac12\varepsilon^\top H_f\varepsilon+\text{higher-order terms}.$$
Squaring and keeping terms through second order in the noise gives
$$L(x+\varepsilon)\approx\frac12r^2+r a^\top\varepsilon
+\frac12(a^\top\varepsilon)^2+\frac r2\varepsilon^\top H_f\varepsilon.$$
Terms such as $(a^\top\varepsilon)(\varepsilon^\top H_f\varepsilon)$ are third order; the squared quadratic term is fourth order.

#### 4 · Take the second-order expectation
Using $\mathbb E\varepsilon=0$ and $\mathbb E[\varepsilon^\top A\varepsilon]=\operatorname{tr}(A\Sigma_\varepsilon)$,
$$\mathbb E[L(x+\varepsilon)]\approx L(x)
+\frac12a^\top\Sigma_\varepsilon a
+\frac r2\operatorname{tr}(H_f\Sigma_\varepsilon).$$
For isotropic noise, the extra terms are $\sigma^2\|\nabla f\|^2/2$ **and** $\sigma^2r\operatorname{tr}(H_f)/2$. The second term need not be nonnegative. Thus a nonlinear noisy objective is not generally exactly Ridge, nor solely a gradient-norm penalty. The expansion needs sufficiently small noise and smoothness; the linear identity above is exact.

title: Early stopping as spectral regularization
summary: Go beyond patience: understand which directions are learned early and why the stopping set is part of model selection.

derivations.title: Solve gradient descent in every singular direction, step by step
derivations.search:
**Setting.** Use $L(\beta)=\|y-X\beta\|^2/2$, constant step $\eta>0$, and $\beta_0=0$. Let $X=U_rD_rV_r^\top$ contain only positive singular values $d_j$. These assumptions are essential: a nonzero initialization leaves an additional term.

#### 1 · Write the affine parameter recurrence
$$\beta_{t+1}=(I-\eta X^\top X)\beta_t+\eta X^\top y.$$
The gradient is $X^\top X\beta_t-X^\top y$; subtracting it gives the two terms above.

#### 2 · Rotate into independent scalar recurrences
Let $a_t=V_r^\top\beta_t$ and $c=U_r^\top y$. Multiplying by $V_r^\top$ gives
$$a_{t+1,j}=(1-\eta d_j^2)a_{t,j}+\eta d_jc_j.$$
Set $q_j=1-\eta d_j^2$. Starting at zero,
$$a_{1,j}=\eta d_jc_j,\quad a_{2,j}=\eta d_jc_j(1+q_j),\quad
 a_{t,j}=\eta d_jc_j\sum_{s=0}^{t-1}q_j^s.$$

#### 3 · Evaluate the geometric sum
Multiply $S=1+q+\cdots+q^{t-1}$ by $q$ and subtract: $(1-q)S=1-q^t$. Here $1-q_j=\eta d_j^2$, so
$$a_{t,j}=\eta d_jc_j\frac{1-q_j^t}{\eta d_j^2}
=\frac{1-(1-\eta d_j^2)^t}{d_j}c_j.$$
Consequently
$$\beta_t=V_r\operatorname{diag}\left(\frac{1-(1-\eta d_j^2)^t}{d_j}\right)U_r^\top y.$$
Zero-singular-value directions remain zero from this initialization; they must not be handled by literal division by zero.

#### 4 · Distinguish stability from monotone shrinkage
Convergence in every represented direction requires $|1-\eta d_j^2|<1$, or $0<\eta<2/d_{\max}^2$. To have $0\le q_j<1$ and filter $s_t(d_j)=1-q_j^t$ rise monotonically from zero toward one, the stronger bound $0<\eta\le1/d_{\max}^2$ is sufficient. In the larger stable interval, a filter can oscillate above and below one.

#### 5 · Compare with Ridge quantitatively
Ridge’s fitted-value factor is $s_\lambda(d)=d^2/(d^2+\lambda)$. Matching one direction at a time would require
$$\lambda_j(t)=d_j^2\frac{1-s_t(d_j)}{s_t(d_j)}
=d_j^2\frac{q_j^t}{1-q_j^t}.$$
For $t>0$ in the monotone regime this is nonnegative, but depends on $j$. A single stopping time does not generally correspond to one common Ridge penalty. The shared idea is preferential suppression of weakly identified directions, not equality of estimators.

title: Sparse representations and dropout
summary: Distinguish sparse parameters, sparse codes, and temporary random activation masks.

derivations.title: Differentiate the sparse-activation KL penalty all the way to one activation
derivations.search:
**Setting.** A hidden unit has activations $a_1,\ldots,a_B\in(0,1)$ and empirical mean $\hat\rho=B^{-1}\sum_i a_i$. A target activity $\rho\in(0,1)$ is fixed. Bernoulli KL requires both probabilities to lie strictly between zero and one for this finite formula.

#### 1 · Write the two possible Bernoulli outcomes
For outcome one the probabilities are $\rho$ and $\hat\rho$; for outcome zero they are $1-\rho$ and $1-\hat\rho$. By the definition of discrete KL,
$$K(\hat\rho)=\rho\log\frac\rho{\hat\rho}+(1-\rho)\log\frac{1-\rho}{1-\hat\rho}.$$

#### 2 · Separate constant and variable logarithms
$$K=\rho\log\rho-\rho\log\hat\rho+(1-\rho)\log(1-\rho)-(1-\rho)\log(1-\hat\rho).$$
Differentiate with respect to $\hat\rho$:
$$K'(\hat\rho)=-\frac\rho{\hat\rho}+\frac{1-\rho}{1-\hat\rho}
=\frac{\hat\rho-\rho}{\hat\rho(1-\hat\rho)}.$$
The denominator is positive, so the derivative points toward the target mean.

#### 3 · Verify the minimum
The derivative is zero at $\hat\rho=\rho$, and
$$K''(\hat\rho)=\frac\rho{\hat\rho^2}+\frac{1-\rho}{(1-\hat\rho)^2}>0.$$
Thus this is the unique minimum, with KL equal to zero.

#### 4 · Continue through averaging and an activation
Since $\partial\hat\rho/\partial a_i=1/B$,
$$\frac{\partial K}{\partial a_i}=\frac1B\left[-\frac\rho{\hat\rho}+\frac{1-\rho}{1-\hat\rho}\right].$$
If $a_i=\sigma(z_i)$, multiply by $a_i(1-a_i)$ to obtain $\partial K/\partial z_i$. A total objective weighted by $\gamma$ multiplies this contribution by $\gamma$. Every example contributes to the shared mean, so this regularizer couples observations in a batch.

#### 5 · Do not apply the probability formula blindly
An unconstrained ReLU activation can exceed one, so its average is not automatically a Bernoulli probability. Use a compatible bounded activation/statistic or a different sparsity penalty. Clamping for numerical safety changes gradients at the clamped boundary and should be explicit.

derivations.title: Derive dropout’s mean, variance, and a nonlinear counterexample
derivations.search:
**Setting.** Treat an activation $h$ as fixed and draw $m\sim\operatorname{Bernoulli}(q)$, with keep probability $0<q\le1$. Inverted dropout returns $\tilde h=mh/q$. The case $q=0$ is excluded from this analytic scaling formula.

#### 1 · Evaluate the two possible values
With probability $q$, $\tilde h=h/q$. With probability $1-q$, $\tilde h=0$. Hence
$$\mathbb E[\tilde h]=q\frac hq+(1-q)0=h.$$

#### 2 · Calculate the second moment, then the variance
$$\mathbb E[\tilde h^2]=q\frac{h^2}{q^2}=\frac{h^2}{q},$$
$$\operatorname{Var}(\tilde h)=\mathbb E[\tilde h^2]-\mathbb E[\tilde h]^2
=\frac{1-q}{q}h^2.$$
At $q=1/2$, the two values are $0$ and $2h$, with mean $h$ and variance $h^2$.

#### 3 · Pass the noise through a linear output
For independent masks $m_j$ and $s=\sum_jw_jm_jh_j/q$, linearity gives $\mathbb E[s]=\sum_jw_jh_j$. Independence makes cross covariances zero, so
$$\operatorname{Var}(s)=\frac{1-q}{q}\sum_jw_j^2h_j^2.$$
For squared loss and fixed target $y$,
$$\mathbb E[(s-y)^2]=(\mathbb E[s]-y)^2+\operatorname{Var}(s).$$
In this particular linear-output case, dropout adds a feature-dependent quadratic penalty. It is not a universal single L2 coefficient for an entire nonlinear network.

#### 4 · Show why the full deterministic network need not equal the stochastic mean
Take $h=1$, $q=1/2$, and a following transformation $f(u)=\operatorname{ReLU}(u-1)$. The stochastic outputs are $f(0)=0$ and $f(2)=1$, so $\mathbb E[f(\tilde h)]=1/2$. But $f(\mathbb E[\tilde h])=f(1)=0$.
Preserving a layer’s activation mean does **not** allow expectation to pass through every later nonlinearity.

#### 5 · Connect the identity to evaluation behavior
Ordinary inverted-dropout evaluation uses the unchanged activation $h$ instead of resampling and does not multiply it by $q$ again. This matches the layerwise scaling convention, not an exact integration over all possible nonlinear subnetworks.

**Setting.** At a fixed input, let $F_1,\ldots,F_M$ be predictions varying over model fitting. Assume all have variance $\sigma^2$ and distinct pairs have covariance $\rho\sigma^2$. Let $\bar F=M^{-1}\sum_mF_m$ and $\mu_m=\mathbb E[F_m]$. Then
$$\bar F-\mathbb E[\bar F]=\frac1M\sum_m(F_m-\mu_m).$$

$$\operatorname{Var}(\bar F)=\frac1{M^2}\sum_{i=1}^M\sum_{j=1}^M
\mathbb E[(F_i-\mu_i)(F_j-\mu_j)].$$
There are $M$ diagonal terms with $i=j$, each equal to $\sigma^2$. There are $M(M-1)$ ordered off-diagonal terms, each equal to $\rho\sigma^2$. Counting ordered pairs is why no extra factor of two is needed.

$$\operatorname{Var}(\bar F)=\frac{M\sigma^2+M(M-1)\rho\sigma^2}{M^2}

$$-\frac1{M-1}\le\rho\le1.$$
A fixed negative correlation cannot persist unchanged as $M$ grows without bound. The often-quoted nonzero limiting floor assumes a feasible fixed nonnegative $\rho$.

#### 5 · Return to prediction error
Variance reduction is only one term of squared prediction risk. Biased models can retain shared bias after averaging, and independent future observation noise remains irreducible. Diversity is useful when it lowers the relevant error covariance without making the component predictions excessively poor.

**Setting.** Let model errors $e\in\mathbb R^M$ be unbiased with positive-definite covariance $\Sigma$. Require $\mathbf1^\top w=1$ so a common target level is preserved. Initially allow negative weights.

$$\mathbb E[(w^\top e)^2]=\mathbb E[w^\top ee^\top w]
=w^\top\mathbb E[ee^\top]w=w^\top\Sigma w.$$

#### 2 · Introduce the equality constraint
Use the Lagrangian
$$\mathcal L(w,\nu)=w^\top\Sigma w-\nu(\mathbf1^\top w-1).$$
For symmetric $\Sigma$, entrywise differentiation of $\sum_{ij}w_i\Sigma_{ij}w_j$ gives $2\Sigma w$, so stationarity requires $2\Sigma w-\nu\mathbf1=0$.

#### 3 · Solve for the multiplier
Because $\Sigma$ is invertible,
$$w=\frac\nu2\Sigma^{-1}\mathbf1.$$
Substitute into $\mathbf1^\top w=1$:
$$\frac\nu2\mathbf1^\top\Sigma^{-1}\mathbf1=1
\quad\Rightarrow\quad\frac\nu2=\frac1{\mathbf1^\top\Sigma^{-1}\mathbf1}.$$
Hence
$$w^*=\frac{\Sigma^{-1}\mathbf1}{\mathbf1^\top\Sigma^{-1}\mathbf1}.$$
Positive definiteness makes the quadratic strictly convex, so this feasible stationary point is the unique optimum.

#### 4 · Obtain the minimum value
Put $c=\mathbf1^\top\Sigma^{-1}\mathbf1$. Then
$$w^{*\top}\Sigma w^*=\frac{\mathbf1^\top\Sigma^{-1}\Sigma\Sigma^{-1}\mathbf1}{c^2}=\frac c{c^2}=\frac1c.$$
This quantifies why error covariance, rather than just each marginal variance, matters.

If errors have mean vector $b$, then $\mathbb E[ee^\top]=\Sigma+bb^\top$ and
$$\mathbb E[(w^\top e)^2]=w^\top\Sigma w+(w^\top b)^2.$$

**Setting.** Fix training points and regard the current fitted values $F_i=F(x_i)$ as coordinates of a vector. Use empirical loss $J(F)=\sum_i(y_i-F_i)^2/(2n)$. A new weak learner $h$ will provide a structured direction in this prediction space.

#### 1 · Differentiate with respect to a fitted value
$$\frac{\partial J}{\partial F_i}=\frac1{2n}\,2(y_i-F_i)(-1)=\frac{F_i-y_i}{n}.$$
The negative gradient is $(y_i-F_i)/n$. Apart from the shared constant $1/n$, it is the residual $r_i=y_i-F_i$.

#### 2 · Approximate that direction with a learner
A weak learner cannot choose arbitrary values independently at every training point. Fitting it to targets $r_i$ approximates the negative-gradient direction using its restricted function family, for example shallow trees.

#### 3 · Derive the best step along a fixed fitted learner
Let $h_i=h(x_i)$ and consider $F_i+\gamma h_i$. Then
$$J(\gamma)=\frac1{2n}\sum_i(r_i-\gamma h_i)^2,$$
$$J'(\gamma)=-\frac1n\sum_i h_i(r_i-\gamma h_i).$$
Set this to zero. If $\sum_i h_i^2>0$, the minimizing step is
$$\gamma^*=\frac{\sum_i h_ir_i}{\sum_i h_i^2}.$$
A learning-rate factor $0<\eta\le1$ may shrink this to the update $F\leftarrow F+\eta\gamma^*h$.

#### 4 · Separate this from bagging
The new residuals depend on previous learners, so boosting is sequential. Bagging fits perturbed versions of a base problem and averages predictions instead. For other differentiable losses, the pseudo-residual is the negative derivative of that loss, not necessarily $y_i-F_i$.

title: Architectures as information flow
summary: Use the supplied guide’s organizing question: how does information move through the model?
search:
Separate structure, routing, and objective The architecture guide distinguishes three choices: the structure of the data, the information-routing rule, and the prediction objective. Models can use the same loss while moving information in very different ways. A sequence contains meaningful order. A graph specifies relations that are not generally a simple sequence. A vector or image can be compressed through a latent representation. The appropriate architecture encodes assumptions about which interactions should be easy to represent. The source’s central question is how does information move? That question gives a more stable mental map than a list of model acronyms. The source’s conceptual map Family Routing mechanism Persistent or intermediate representation RNN Reuse a state transition across time Hidden state LSTM / GRU Gate the state update Cell/hidden state or one gated state Encoder–decoder Encode a source, decode a target Context or source memory Autoencoder Compress and reconstruct Latent code Transformer Content-dependent token interaction Contextual token representations GNN Pass messages along edges Node representations GAT Learn weights over graph neighbors Attention-weighted node representations There is no strict hierarchy in which each newer family replaces all earlier ones. The models express different inductive biases, and some solve different training objectives altogether. Choose the architecture by the available relationships For a streaming sequence, a recurrent state naturally carries information from the past. A bidirectional recurrent model uses future context too; that can be useful offline and invalid when future inputs are unavailable at prediction time. For a long sequence with content-dependent interactions, attention offers direct access to allowed source positions. The cost of dense pairwise interactions grows with sequence length, so the routing benefit comes with a computational trade-off. For relational data, a graph model uses the given neighborhood rather than flattening every entity into unrelated rows. Its usefulness depends on graph construction, edge direction, self-loops, and whether the split matches deployment. An autoencoder is appropriate when reconstruction or a latent representation is the objective. If labels for a downstream task are available, good reconstruction does not automatically mean the representation is best for that task. Roles can be combined The guide gives LSTM autoencoders, temporal GNNs, graph Transformers, and encoders feeding relational models as examples of hybrids. These are not exceptions to the map: each component contributes a routing or representation role. A residual connection and an LSTM cell path share an optimization theme: preserve a relatively direct route and learn modifications around it. Gates and attention both select information, but at different granularities. A gate scales state coordinates; attention assigns weights across candidate source representations. Every autoencoder has an encoder, but a classifier’s encoder does not make it an autoencoder. Distinguishing architectural roles from training objectives prevents several common study confusions. Complexity is not just parameter count Two models with similar parameter counts can have very different computational structure. Recurrence has a sequential dependency chain. Dense attention has pairwise interactions and parallel training across positions. Graph models operate on the selected edges and can create a different batching problem for variable-size graphs. The source asks for comparison under the same split and metric, including training time, inference cost, robustness, and data regime. The architecture should earn its complexity by improving the intended procedure rather than merely having greater expressiveness. Step by step Derive receptive reach from repeated local information routing Setting. Let A be a nonnegative adjacency matrix describing allowed one-step messages between n positions or nodes. Ignore nonlinearities for the first calculation so the support of information flow is easy to inspect. This is a structural derivation, not a claim that every allowed influence is learned or useful. 1 · Expand one and two propagation steps For scalar input features x , one step gives h^{(1)}=Ax , with h^{(1)}_i=\sum_jA_{ij}x_j . A second gives h^{(2)}_i=\sum_jA_{ij}h^{(1)}_j
=\sum_j\sum_kA_{ij}A_{jk}x_k
=\sum_k(A^2)_{ik}x_k. A term A_{ij}A_{jk} is nonzero only when information can travel from k through j to i . 2 · Extend by induction If h^{(L)}=A^Lx , then h^{(L+1)}=Ah^{(L)}=A^{L+1}x . For an unweighted graph, (A^L)_{ik} counts walks of length L from k to i . Including self-loops lets shorter paths be padded with “stay” steps, giving access within at most L hops. 3 · Restore learned transformations A local message-passing layer can transform and nonlinearly combine its inputs, but without an extra long-range connection its output still depends only on its allowed neighbors. Repeated composition expands the possible dependency set by another hop per layer. Cancellation, learned zero weights, or compression can make the actual dependence smaller than this structural bound. 4 · Compare recurrence and unrestricted attention In a recurrent chain, an input at time k reaches time T through T-k transitions. Dense attention permits a direct edge between any allowed pair in one layer, while causal or local masks remove edges. derivations.title: Derive receptive reach from repeated local information routing
derivations.search:
**Setting.** Let $A$ be a nonnegative adjacency matrix describing allowed one-step messages between $n$ positions or nodes. Ignore nonlinearities for the first calculation so the support of information flow is easy to inspect. This is a structural derivation, not a claim that every allowed influence is learned or useful.

#### 1 · Expand one and two propagation steps
For scalar input features $x$, one step gives $h^{(1)}=Ax$, with $h^{(1)}_i=\sum_jA_{ij}x_j$. A second gives
$$h^{(2)}_i=\sum_jA_{ij}h^{(1)}_j
=\sum_j\sum_kA_{ij}A_{jk}x_k
=\sum_k(A^2)_{ik}x_k.$$
A term $A_{ij}A_{jk}$ is nonzero only when information can travel from $k$ through $j$ to $i$.

#### 2 · Extend by induction
If $h^{(L)}=A^Lx$, then $h^{(L+1)}=Ah^{(L)}=A^{L+1}x$. For an unweighted graph, $(A^L)_{ik}$ counts walks of length $L$ from $k$ to $i$. Including self-loops lets shorter paths be padded with “stay” steps, giving access within at most $L$ hops.

#### 3 · Restore learned transformations
A local message-passing layer can transform and nonlinearly combine its inputs, but without an extra long-range connection its output still depends only on its allowed neighbors. Repeated composition expands the possible dependency set by another hop per layer. Cancellation, learned zero weights, or compression can make the actual dependence smaller than this structural bound.

#### 4 · Compare recurrence and unrestricted attention
In a recurrent chain, an input at time $k$ reaches time $T$ through $T-k$ transitions. Dense attention permits a direct edge between any allowed pair in one layer, while causal or local masks remove edges. This changes dependency path length, not a guarantee of successful memory or reasoning.

#### 5 · Keep computation separate from parameter sharing
Repeating the same recurrent cell for $T$ steps multiplies its compute and activation-storage needs but not the number of distinct cell parameters. Unrestricted attention has $T^2$ candidate interactions per head. A sparse graph with $|E|$ edges has an edge-dependent propagation cost. Equal parameter counts therefore do not imply equal memory use, sequential depth, or runtime.

derivations.title: Derive BPTT, Jacobian order, and shared-parameter gradients
derivations.search:
**Setting.** Let $a_t=W_xx_t+W_hh_{t-1}+b$, $h_t=\phi(a_t)$, and $L=\sum_{t=1}^T\ell_t(h_t)$. Treat $h_0$ as fixed. All gradients below are **column vectors**. Let $D_t=\operatorname{diag}(\phi'(a_t))$ and $u_t=\nabla_{h_t}\ell_t$ be the direct loss contribution at step $t$.

#### 1 · Derive the one-step state Jacobian
The affine derivative is $\partial a_t/\partial h_{t-1}=W_h$. The elementwise activation derivative is $\partial h_t/\partial a_t=D_t$. Applying the chain rule gives
$$J_t=\frac{\partial h_t}{\partial h_{t-1}}=D_tW_h.$$
Matrix order matters: first $W_h$ acts on a perturbation, then $D_t$ scales its output coordinates.

#### 2 · Add the direct and future loss paths
The total gradient $g_t=\nabla_{h_t}L$ receives the direct contribution $u_t$ and the contribution through $h_{t+1}$:
$$g_t=u_t+J_{t+1}^\top g_{t+1},\qquad g_T=u_T.$$
This is reverse-mode differentiation on a graph with two outgoing routes from $h_t$.

#### 3 · Expand two steps to fix the product order
$$g_k=u_k+J_{k+1}^\top u_{k+1}+J_{k+1}^\top J_{k+2}^\top g_{k+2}.$$
Continuing gives, for a loss **only at the final step**,
$$g_k=J_{k+1}^\top J_{k+2}^\top\cdots J_T^\top g_T.$$
Equivalently, using row gradients gives $g_k^\top=g_T^\top J_TJ_{T-1}\cdots J_{k+1}$. An ascending unqualified product after a row gradient would be ambiguous or wrong because these Jacobians do not generally commute.

#### 4 · Move from state gradients to pre-activation gradients
Define $\delta_t=\nabla_{a_t}L=D_tg_t$. Since $J_{t+1}^\top=W_h^\top D_{t+1}$,
$$\delta_t=(u_t+W_h^\top\delta_{t+1})\odot\phi'(a_t),\qquad\delta_{T+1}=0.$$
The recurrence includes every direct loss and every future contribution once.

#### 5 · Sum every occurrence of each shared parameter
For entry $(W_h)_{ij}$ at time $t$, $\partial a_{t,i}/\partial(W_h)_{ij}=h_{t-1,j}$. Because the same parameter appears at all times, the chain rule sums these local contributions:
$$\nabla_{W_h}L=\sum_{t=1}^T\delta_th_{t-1}^\top,\qquad
\nabla_{W_x}L=\sum_{t=1}^T\delta_tx_t^\top,\qquad
\nabla_bL=\sum_{t=1}^T\delta_t.$$
Future dependence of $h_{t-1}$ is already handled through the reverse recurrence; adding it separately again would double count.

#### 6 · Interpret truncation
Detaching a boundary hidden state removes the derivative paths through earlier chunks. Its numerical value can still carry history forward, but losses in the current chunk no longer update parameters through those earlier operations. Truncated BPTT is therefore an approximation to the full-sequence gradient, not merely a different memory allocation.

$$a_1=0.8(1)+0.6(0)=0.8,\qquad h_1=\tanh(0.8)\approx0.6640368.$$

A state value near zero is not itself proof that an earlier input has no influence. Values measure the current output; derivatives measure sensitivity to perturbations. Conversely, a nonzero hidden state is not proof that sensitivity to distant inputs remains strong.

title: LSTM gates and memory timescales
summary: Understand the additive cell path, each gate’s role, and the limits of the memory analogy.
search:
Two states with different roles An LSTM introduces a cell state c_t in addition to the hidden output h_t . The cell provides an additive route for storing and modifying information. The hidden state exposes a gated transformation of that cell to the rest of the network. For concatenated input u_t=[h_{t-1};x_t] , the source defines f_t=\sigma(W_fu_t+b_f),\qquad i_t=\sigma(W_iu_t+b_i), \tilde c_t=\tanh(W_cu_t+b_c),\qquad
c_t=f_t\odot c_{t-1}+i_t\odot\tilde c_t, o_t=\sigma(W_ou_t+b_o),\qquad h_t=o_t\odot\tanh(c_t). The forget gate retains or attenuates old cell content. The input gate controls new candidate content. The output gate controls how much transformed cell content is exposed as the hidden state. These sigmoid-valued gates are continuous controls, not discrete instructions or class probabilities. Why the additive path matters A vanilla recurrent state repeatedly passes through a full nonlinear transformation. The LSTM cell instead contains a direct additive term from the previous cell. For a standard cell without peepholes, hold the previous hidden-state coordinate h_{t-1} fixed while differentiating the cell-state coordinate. The direct block is \left.\frac{\partial c_t}{\partial c_{t-1}}\right|_{h_{t-1}\ \mathrm{fixed}}=\operatorname{diag}(f_t). Over several steps, that particular direct path scales coordinatewise as a product of the realized forget gates. When those values stay close to one, the path can retain useful sensitivity rather than repeatedly crush it through saturation. The qualification is essential: the total derivative contains additional paths because the gates depend on recurrent variables. The source’s approximation isolates the memory-path intuition; the block form above makes that scope precise. It is not the full Jacobian of the joint cell and hidden state. The source’s constant-forget-gate illustration. A gate near one retains a much larger fraction over time than a small gate; real gates vary with input and state. At a fixed input, gates f,i,o and candidate g depend on the previous hidden state h , while c'=f(h)\odot c+i(h)\odot g(h),\qquad h'=o(h)\odot\tanh(c'). Treat previous cell c and hidden state h as independent coordinates of the recurrent state s=(c,h) when forming its local Jacobian. 1 · Hold the hidden-state coordinate fixed If h is fixed, the gate values do not change when c changes. For coordinates j,k , \frac{\partial c'_j}{\partial c_k}=f_j\,\mathbf1_{j=k}. Therefore the direct cell-to-cell block is F=\operatorname{diag}(f) , not the vector f itself. 2 · Include the routes through the gates Let J_f=\partial f/\partial h , with analogous definitions for i,g,o . The product rule gives A=\frac{\partial c'}{\partial h}
=\operatorname{diag}(c)J_f+\operatorname{diag}(g)J_i+\operatorname{diag}(i)J_g. These terms exist because changing the previous hidden state changes forgetting, writing, and candidate content. 3 · Differentiate the exposed hidden state Let T=\operatorname{diag}(o\odot[1-\tanh^2(c')]) . Then \frac{\partial h'}{\partial c}=TF, \frac{\partial h'}{\partial h}=TA+\operatorname{diag}(\tanh(c'))J_o. The first contribution passes through the updated cell; the second passes directly through the output gate. 4 · Assemble the full transition Jacobian \frac{\partial(c',h')}{\partial(c,h)}=
\begin{bmatrix}
F&A\\ TF&TA+\operatorname{diag}(\tanh(c'))J_o
\end{bmatrix}. Across time, gradients involve products of these full block matrices. The product of forget gates describes one additive cell path, not the entire derivative of the recurrent computation. 5 · Interpret the benefit without overclaiming Along the direct path, factors near one can preserve sensitivity without repeatedly multiplying by an arbitrary recurrent matrix and a tanh derivative. This eases a particular source of vanishing gradients. Other paths, saturation, gate dynamics, and optimization still matter, so an LSTM does not guarantee nonvanishing total gradients or unlimited memory. k=\frac{\log r}{\log f}. The half-life is k_{1/2}=\log(1/2)/\log f : approximately 1 step for f=0.5 , 6.58 for 0.9 , and 68.97 for 0.99 . \bar i_t=\bar c_t\odot g_t,\quad
\bar g_t=\bar c_t\odot i_t, \bar o_t=\bar h_t\odot\tanh(c_t),\qquad

There are four affine maps: three gates plus a candidate transformation. Official PyTorch supplement. It computes four affine transformations: input, forget, candidate, and output. 1 · Count one transformation in the mathematical convention A transformation of concatenated [h_{t-1};x_t]\in\mathbb R^{h+d} to h outputs has h(h+d) weights and h biases. Four transformations therefore have 4[h(h+d)+h]=4h(d+h+1) parameters in the single-bias convention used by the source. 2 · Count the tensors in the PyTorch convention For one layer, the input weight tensor has shape (4h,d) and contains 4hd values. The recurrent weight tensor has shape (4h,h) and contains 4h^2 values. With biases enabled, two bias vectors each have length 4h . Hence N=4hd+4h^2+8h=4h(d+h+2). Adding the two bias vectors is functionally equivalent to one effective bias, but the library stores two trainable tensors. 3 · Verify a small example For d=3,h=5 , the four counts are 60 , 100 , 20 , and 20 , totaling 200 . The single-bias mathematical count is 4(5)(3+5+1)=180 . The difference is the additional 20 -element bias vector. 4 · State what is outside this formula An output head adds its own parameters. Stacked layers receive the previous layer’s output width; bidirectionality changes that width and adds a second direction; an LSTM projection changes recurrent shapes and adds projection weights. Sequence length and batch size do not multiply the number of shared parameters. **Setting.** Consider a standard LSTM without peephole connections. At a fixed input, gates $f,i,o$ and candidate $g$ depend on the previous hidden state $h$, while
$$c'=f(h)\odot c+i(h)\odot g(h),\qquad h'=o(h)\odot\tanh(c').$$

#### 1 · Hold the hidden-state coordinate fixed
If $h$ is fixed, the gate values do not change when $c$ changes. For coordinates $j,k$,
$$\frac{\partial c'_j}{\partial c_k}=f_j\,\mathbf1_{j=k}.$$
Therefore the **direct cell-to-cell block** is $F=\operatorname{diag}(f)$, not the vector $f$ itself.

#### 2 · Include the routes through the gates
Let $J_f=\partial f/\partial h$, with analogous definitions for $i,g,o$. The product rule gives
$$A=\frac{\partial c'}{\partial h}
=\operatorname{diag}(c)J_f+\operatorname{diag}(g)J_i+\operatorname{diag}(i)J_g.$$
These terms exist because changing the previous hidden state changes forgetting, writing, and candidate content.

#### 3 · Differentiate the exposed hidden state

$$\frac{\partial h'}{\partial c}=TF,$$
$$\frac{\partial h'}{\partial h}=TA+\operatorname{diag}(\tanh(c'))J_o.$$
The first contribution passes through the updated cell; the second passes directly through the output gate.

#### 4 · Assemble the full transition Jacobian
$$\frac{\partial(c',h')}{\partial(c,h)}=
\begin{bmatrix}
F&A\\ TF&TA+\operatorname{diag}(\tanh(c'))J_o
\end{bmatrix}.$$
Across time, gradients involve products of these full block matrices. The product of forget gates describes one additive cell path, not the entire derivative of the recurrent computation.

#### 5 · Interpret the benefit without overclaiming
Along the direct path, factors near one can preserve sensitivity without repeatedly multiplying by an arbitrary recurrent matrix and a tanh derivative. This eases a particular source of vanishing gradients. Other paths, saturation, gate dynamics, and optimization still matter, so an LSTM does not guarantee nonvanishing total gradients or unlimited memory.

derivations.title: Unroll cell memory, derive its half-life, and differentiate a gate update
derivations.search:
**Setting.** First use scalar cell updates $c_t=f_tc_{t-1}+u_t$, where $u_t=i_tg_t$ is the newly written content. Treat the realized gates as given for the direct-path calculation.

#### 1 · Unroll the first two updates
$$c_1=f_1c_0+u_1,$$
$$c_2=f_2(f_1c_0+u_1)+u_2=f_2f_1c_0+f_2u_1+u_2.$$
At step $t$, continuing the substitution gives
$$c_t=\left(\prod_{j=1}^tf_j\right)c_0+
\sum_{k=1}^t\left(\prod_{j=k+1}^tf_j\right)u_k.$$
The empty product for $k=t$ is one. Each write is discounted by the forget gates encountered **after** it was written.

#### 2 · Solve a constant-gate retention question
If all $f_j=f$ with $0<f<1$, a write retained for $k$ transitions is multiplied by $f^k$. To retain fraction $r\in(0,1)$, solve
$$f^k=r\quad\Rightarrow\quad k\log f=\log r\quad\Rightarrow\quad
k=\frac{\log r}{\log f}.$$
The half-life is $k_{1/2}=\log(1/2)/\log f$: approximately $1$ step for $f=0.5$, $6.58$ for $0.9$, and $68.97$ for $0.99$. This is a direct-path timescale, not an empirical memory guarantee.

#### 3 · Differentiate the local gate operations
Suppose the incoming reverse gradients are $\bar h_t$ through $h_t=o_t\odot\tanh(c_t)$ and $\bar c_t^{\rm other}$ through other downstream cell routes. Add their contributions:
$$\bar c_t=\bar c_t^{\rm other}+\bar h_t\odot o_t\odot[1-\tanh^2(c_t)].$$
The elementwise product rule then gives
$$\bar f_t=\bar c_t\odot c_{t-1},\quad
\bar i_t=\bar c_t\odot g_t,\quad
\bar g_t=\bar c_t\odot i_t,$$
$$\bar o_t=\bar h_t\odot\tanh(c_t),\qquad
\bar c_{t-1}^{\rm direct}=\bar c_t\odot f_t.$$

#### 4 · Continue through each gate nonlinearity
For sigmoid gate pre-activations $a_f,a_i,a_o$ and tanh candidate $a_g$,
$$\bar a_f=\bar f_t\odot f_t\odot(1-f_t),\quad
\bar a_i=\bar i_t\odot i_t\odot(1-i_t),$$
$$\bar a_o=\bar o_t\odot o_t\odot(1-o_t),\quad
\bar a_g=\bar g_t\odot(1-g_t^2).$$
Their affine weight gradients are outer products of these signals with the corresponding concatenated input. Their contributions to $h_{t-1}$ are summed. These are the same local chain-rule operations as in an ordinary feed-forward network, arranged around an additive memory path.

derivations.title: Count recurrent weights and distinguish one bias from two
derivations.search:
**Setting.** A single unidirectional, unprojected LSTM layer has input width $d$ and hidden width $h$. It computes four affine transformations: input, forget, candidate, and output.

#### 1 · Count one transformation in the mathematical convention
A transformation of concatenated $[h_{t-1};x_t]\in\mathbb R^{h+d}$ to $h$ outputs has $h(h+d)$ weights and $h$ biases. Four transformations therefore have
$$4[h(h+d)+h]=4h(d+h+1)$$
parameters in the single-bias convention used by the source.

#### 2 · Count the tensors in the PyTorch convention
For one layer, the input weight tensor has shape $(4h,d)$ and contains $4hd$ values. The recurrent weight tensor has shape $(4h,h)$ and contains $4h^2$ values. With biases enabled, two bias vectors each have length $4h$. Hence
$$N=4hd+4h^2+8h=4h(d+h+2).$$
Adding the two bias vectors is functionally equivalent to one effective bias, but the library stores two trainable tensors.

#### 3 · Verify a small example
For $d=3,h=5$, the four counts are $60$, $100$, $20$, and $20$, totaling $200$. The single-bias mathematical count is $4(5)(3+5+1)=180$. The difference is the additional $20$-element bias vector.

#### 4 · State what is outside this formula
An output head adds its own parameters. Stacked layers receive the previous layer’s output width; bidirectionality changes that width and adds a second direction; an LSTM projection changes recurrent shapes and adds projection weights. Sequence length and batch size do not multiply the number of shared parameters. The vanilla RNN and GRU analogues replace four affine blocks with one and three, respectively, under the same assumptions.

title: GRUs and gate conventions
summary: Understand a single gated state, then keep the PDF and PyTorch equations explicitly distinct.
search:
A compact gated state The GRU combines the roles of the LSTM’s cell and hidden state into one principal recurrent state. The source uses an update gate z_t and a reset gate r_t : z_t=\sigma(W_zx_t+U_zh_{t-1}+b_z), r_t=\sigma(W_rx_t+U_rh_{t-1}+b_r), \tilde h_t=\tanh(W_hx_t+U_h(r_t\odot h_{t-1})+b_h), h_t=(1-z_t)\odot h_{t-1}+z_t\odot\tilde h_t. In this PDF convention , a larger update gate moves the state more strongly toward the candidate. The reset gate controls how previous-state information enters the candidate computation. The final interpolation creates an additive route between old and new information. That is the connection to LSTM memory-path reasoning, despite the different state organization. Work the source’s interpolation Let h_{t-1}=0.6 , z_t=0.25 , and the already-computed candidate be \tilde h_t=-0.2 . Then h_t=0.75(0.6)+0.25(-0.2)=0.40. The old state dominates because the source’s update gate is small. The example also lists a reset-gate value, but once the candidate has already been supplied, the reset value does not enter this final arithmetic again. This separates two questions: how to construct the candidate, and how strongly to replace the state with it. Compare GRU with LSTM by mechanism Aspect LSTM GRU Main state Cell plus hidden state One hidden state Gates Forget, input, output Reset, update Direct-path intuition Gated cell retention and addition Old/new state interpolation Parameter cost Four affine gate/candidate maps Three affine gate/candidate maps Predictive accuracy Task dependent Task dependent The source does not claim that either must dominate. Fewer gates can reduce cost, but a smaller architecture is not automatically more accurate or easier for every task. Compare them under the same data split and prediction constraints. PyTorch’s documented convention This section is an implementation supplement , not a replacement of the source equations. PyTorch writes the final interpolation as h_t=(1-z_t)\odot n_t+z_t\odot h_{t-1}. Here a large z_t preserves the old state. The label “update gate” therefore has the opposite intuitive direction from the PDF’s displayed interpolation. PyTorch also places the reset multiplication after the hidden affine map in the candidate: n_t=\tanh(W_{in}x_t+b_{in}+r_t\odot(W_{hn}h_{t-1}+b_{hn})). The PDF instead places the reset inside the recurrent multiplication, U_h(r_t\odot h_{t-1}) . In general, U_h(r_t\odot h_{t-1})\ne r_t\odot(U_hh_{t-1}). These are not repaired by simply renaming the gate. The official GRU reference explicitly documents this implementation distinction. It matters when comparing a hand-written cell or paper equation with framework outputs. Step by step Work through GRU interpolation and the noncommuting reset operations Setting. The source writes h'=(1-z_s)\odot h+z_s\odot n . PyTorch writes h'=(1-z_p)\odot n+z_p\odot h . The subscripts explicitly distinguish the gate conventions. 1 · Match the interpolation coefficients The formulas agree for fixed h,n if z_p=1-z_s , because (1-z_p)n+z_ph=z_sn+(1-z_s)h. For h=0.6,n=-0.2,z_s=0.25 , this gives 0.75(0.6)+0.25(-0.2)=0.4 . The matching PyTorch-style gate value is z_p=0.75 , not 0.25 . Equal gate numbers with swapped semantics describe different updates. 2 · Differentiate the interpolation locally In the source convention, holding the other inputs fixed gives \frac{\partial h'}{\partial h}=\operatorname{diag}(1-z_s),\quad
\frac{\partial h'}{\partial n}=\operatorname{diag}(z_s),\quad
\frac{\partial h'}{\partial z_s}=\operatorname{diag}(n-h). These are partial blocks. Since n and z_s themselves depend on h , the total state Jacobian contains additional chain-rule terms. 3 · Compare the reset placement A common textbook candidate uses U(r\odot h)=U\operatorname{diag}(r)h . PyTorch’s candidate uses r\odot(Uh+b_h)=\operatorname{diag}(r)(Uh+b_h) . Even ignoring bias, U\operatorname{diag}(r) and \operatorname{diag}(r)U are generally different matrices. 4 · Calculate a concrete counterexample Let U=\begin{bmatrix}1&2\\3&4\end{bmatrix},\quad
h=\begin{bmatrix}1\\2\end{bmatrix},\quad
r=\begin{bmatrix}0.2\\0.8\end{bmatrix}. Reset first: r\odot h=(0.2,1.6)^\top , so U(r\odot h)=(3.4,7.0)^\top . Transform first: Uh=(5,11)^\top , so r\odot(Uh)=(1.0,8.8)^\top . Subsequent tanh does not remove this difference. 5 · Connect the formulas to implementation comparisons Changing gate names is enough to reconcile opposite interpolation conventions for given gates and candidates. It does not reconcile different candidate computations. The PyTorch GRU documentation explicitly describes its reset placement. Its single-layer, unidirectional bias-enabled parameter count is 3h(d+h+2) , because it stores three input/recurrent affine blocks and two bias vectors per block. Expanded derivation Chapter source · PDF p. 12 Library reference Link to this calculation ↗ A practical sequence-to-sequence use The official translation tutorial uses GRUs in its encoder and decoder, with additive attention and attention visualizations. It is a complete example of the model’s role: recurrent updates build and consume sequence representations, while attention retrieves from source states. When reading the code, follow state shapes, initialization, whether state is reset for independent sequences, and the source of decoder inputs during training versus inference. Those choices determine the actual prediction behavior more than memorizing the number of gates. The portable understanding is the mechanism—candidate construction plus gated interpolation—together with the discipline of checking the exact convention before translating an equation into code.
