title: Encoders, decoders, and teacher forcing
summary: Separate architectural roles from layer types, and distinguish training context from generation context.
search:
Encoder and decoder describe roles An encoder transforms an input into a useful representation. A decoder transforms a representation into an output. Either can use recurrent layers, attention, convolutions, or graph computations. The label specifies information flow, not a particular neuron or layer. In classical recurrent sequence-to-sequence modeling, the encoder processes x_{1:T} into context c . The decoder models p(y_{1:U}\mid x_{1:T})=\prod_{u=1}^{U}p(y_u\mid y_{<u},c). The input and output lengths can differ. At each output step, the model conditions on source information and earlier target tokens. This is different from requiring one output aligned with every input position. Why the autoregressive factorization is useful Rather than produce a whole structured sequence as an unstructured object, the model makes a series of conditional predictions. For observed target sequence y^* , the usual token-level negative log-likelihood is L=-\sum_{u=1}^{U}\log p(y_u^*\mid y_{<u}^*,c). The model is trained to assign high probability to each observed token under the supplied history. The chosen representation, decoder state, and attention mechanism determine how it uses that context. The guide’s translation example maps an encoded source sentence into a sequence of output words. A later word depends on both the source and what has already been generated. This is the important dependency, not the language pair itself. Step by step Derive the autoregressive likelihood and masked token loss Setting. Let x be an observed source sequence and y_1,\ldots,y_U a target sequence, including an end-of-sequence token when termination is modeled. No independence between target tokens is assumed. 1 · Apply the conditional probability product rule For two target tokens, p(y_1,y_2\mid x)=p(y_1\mid x)p(y_2\mid y_1,x). Applying the same rule to a third gives a new factor p(y_3\mid y_1,y_2,x) . Repeating yields p_\theta(y_{1:U}\mid x)=\prod_{u=1}^U p_\theta(y_u\mid y_{<u},x). This factorization is a probability identity. An encoder–decoder supplies a parameterization of its factors; a compressed context may impose an approximation to the full conditioning information. 2 · Convert a product into an additive training objective Take negative natural logarithms: -\log p_\theta(y_{1:U}\mid x)=-\sum_{u=1}^U\log p_\theta(y_u\mid y_{<u},x). The target history in each factor is the observed history. Supplying it during training is teacher forcing, consistent with evaluating the likelihood of the observed sequence. 3 · Expand one categorical token loss For logits z_{u,k} over vocabulary classes k and observed token y_u , -\log p_\theta(y_u\mid y_{<u},x)
=-z_{u,y_u}+\log\sum_k e^{z_{u,k}}. The decoder must receive shifted targets or a mask that prevents the token at u from directly revealing its own answer. 4 · Remove padding without changing the modeled event For a padded batch, let m_{b,u}=1 for genuine target tokens and zero for padding. A mean per-token objective is J=\frac{\sum_{b,u}m_{b,u}\ell_{b,u}}{\sum_{b,u}m_{b,u}}. This requires at least one valid token. Averaging each sequence separately and then averaging sequences gives a different weighting when lengths differ. Both may be deliberate, but the denominator must match the intended objective. 5 · Explain generation separately At generation time, the true prefix is unavailable. The model conditions on generated tokens and chooses or samples the next token until termination. Sampling implements the autoregressive model; greedy or beam decoding is a decision procedure over that model. Parallel teacher-forced training does not make ordinary autoregressive generation nonsequential. Expanded derivation Chapter source · PDF p. 13 Link to this calculation ↗ Teacher forcing During training, true previous tokens are available, so the decoder can receive y_{u-1}^* . This is teacher forcing. At inference it cannot receive an unknown true target token, so it receives its own previous prediction instead. The source calls the resulting mismatch exposure bias : training histories are often cleaner than the histories encountered after an error during free-running generation. This does not make teacher forcing invalid; it identifies a difference between the conditional training calculation and the generation procedure. Teacher forcing also does not give permission to include unavailable future target information. The autoregressive structure still determines which context each prediction is allowed to use. The fixed-context bottleneck An early recurrent encoder–decoder might compress the entire input into one final state. For a long source sequence, that fixed-width representation must carry every detail the decoder will later need. Attention relieves this bottleneck by letting each decoder step retrieve from all encoder states. In the guide’s additive attention, e_{u,t}=v^\top\tanh(W_ss_{u-1}+W_hh_t), \alpha_{u,t}=\frac{e^{e_{u,t}}}{\sum_j e^{e_{u,j}}},\qquad c_u=\sum_t\alpha_{u,t}h_t. Now the context is specific to output step u . The decoder can emphasize different source positions at different stages instead of relying exclusively on one fixed vector. Three architectural forms An encoder-only model contextualizes the available input and can support classification, tagging, retrieval, or embeddings. A decoder-only model uses allowed prior context for autoregressive generation. An encoder–decoder model builds source memory and then generates while consulting it. These are routing forms that can appear with recurrent components or Transformers. “Encoder” is not a synonym for “autoencoder”: reconstruction is a particular training objective discussed in the next chapter. Existing implementation and visualization The official PyTorch translation tutorial already includes an encoder, GRU decoder, teacher forcing logic, additive attention, training code, and labeled attention maps. The resource link points to that complete application, and a separate visualization link goes directly to the attention display section. Use the example to trace what is passed into the decoder at each step, when the true target is used, and how attention weights produce a context vector. Those questions test understanding of the architecture instead of merely whether you can instantiate a recurrent layer.

title: Autoencoders, bottlenecks, and denoising
summary: Understand reconstruction as an objective, and distinguish useful compression from copying or memorization.
search:
Reconstruction defines the task An autoencoder uses an encoder and decoder with the input itself as the usual target: z=f_\theta(x),\qquad\hat x=g_\phi(z). The encoder constructs a code z and the decoder reconstructs the observation. This is not simply “an encoder model”; the paired reconstruction objective is essential to the definition. The source’s encoder–latent-code–decoder diagram. The bottleneck lies in the representation or training constraints, not in the word “encoder” alone. Architectures · PDF p. 15 For continuous data the guide uses squared reconstruction error, for example \lVert x-\hat x\rVert^2/d . For binary or Bernoulli-modeled inputs, a binary cross-entropy reconstruction objective can be appropriate. The likelihood assumptions and feature scales matter. A bottleneck restricts the easy identity map If the latent dimension k is smaller than input dimension d , the autoencoder is undercomplete. It must prioritize information that helps reconstruction. But dimension alone does not guarantee useful semantics: a powerful nonlinear model can still memorize a finite training sample or devote its limited capacity to nuisance variation. The source connects a linear undercomplete autoencoder with squared loss to the principal subspace of PCA. The relationship concerns a reconstruction-optimal subspace, not a guarantee that the learned latent axes have the same orientation or interpretation as a particular PCA basis. A nonlinear decoder can represent curved structure, but additional expressiveness also changes the risks. Good training reconstruction is not enough to establish a useful general representation. Step by step Derive the PCA connection for a linear reconstruction model Setting. Use centered column-vector data x\in\mathbb R^d with finite second moment S=\mathbb E[xx^\top] . Consider an orthogonal rank- k linear reconstruction \hat x=UU^\top x , where U\in\mathbb R^{d\times k} and U^\top U=I . This restricted problem makes the principal-subspace connection explicit. 1 · Expand the reconstruction error Let P=UU^\top . Since P^\top=P and P^2=P , \|x-Px\|^2=x^\top(I-P)^\top(I-P)x=x^\top(I-P)x. The last equality follows from (I-P)^2=I-2P+P^2=I-P . 2 · Take the expectation using a trace For a scalar, x^\top Ax=\operatorname{tr}(Axx^\top) . Therefore \mathbb E\|x-Px\|^2=\operatorname{tr}(S)-\operatorname{tr}(PS)
=\operatorname{tr}(S)-\operatorname{tr}(U^\top SU). The first term is constant. Minimizing error is equivalent to maximizing variance captured by the k -dimensional subspace. 3 · Rotate into covariance eigenvectors Write S=V\Lambda V^\top , with eigenvalues \lambda_1\ge\cdots\ge\lambda_d\ge0 , and put C=V^\top U . Then C^\top C=I and \operatorname{tr}(U^\top SU)=\operatorname{tr}(C^\top\Lambda C)
=\sum_{i=1}^d\lambda_i\sum_{j=1}^k C_{ij}^2. Let a_i=\sum_jC_{ij}^2 . Because CC^\top is an orthogonal projector, 0\le a_i\le1 and \sum_i a_i=k . 4 · Allocate captured dimensions to the largest eigenvalues For ordered eigenvalues, the largest possible weighted sum under those constraints is \sum_{i=1}^k\lambda_i : if weight remains on a smaller eigenvalue while a larger one has available capacity, transferring that weight cannot reduce the sum. Choosing U as the first k eigenvectors attains this bound. Thus the minimum reconstruction error is \sum_{i=k+1}^d\lambda_i . 5 · Avoid claiming unique latent coordinates For unconstrained linear encoder/decoder matrices, the principal reconstruction subspace can be represented in many latent bases. Replacing an encoder by RE and decoder by DR^{-1} for invertible R leaves DE unchanged. An ordinary nonlinear autoencoder therefore neither guarantees PCA coordinates nor solves this exact orthogonal projection problem. The equivalence concerns the optimal linear squared-error reconstruction subspace under appropriate conditions. Expanded derivation Chapter source · PDF p. 15 Link to this calculation ↗ Denoising changes the shortcut A denoising autoencoder sees a corrupted input but reconstructs the clean target: \tilde x\sim q(\tilde x\mid x),\qquad
L=\lVert x-g_\phi(f_\theta(\tilde x))\rVert^2. Copying the noisy input is no longer sufficient. The model is encouraged to preserve stable structure that predicts the clean sample. This only makes sense if the corruption process represents a valid nuisance rather than changes that should alter the desired target. For example, reconstructing a clean signal from a plausible noisy measurement has a clear interpretation. Adding arbitrary noise to strongly constrained features can instead create unrealistic training examples. The augmentation and noise chapter develops that assumption. Step by step Derive the optimal denoising reconstruction under squared error Setting. Let clean data be a random vector X and corrupted input be Z . Train a reconstruction function g by minimizing \mathbb E\|X-g(Z)\|^2 . Assume the relevant conditional second moments exist. The function class is unrestricted for this population argument. 1 · Condition on a particular corrupted observation At Z=z , a proposed reconstruction a=g(z) incurs conditional risk \mathbb E[\|X-a\|^2\mid Z=z] . Define \mu(z)=\mathbb E[X\mid Z=z] . 2 · Add and subtract the conditional mean X-a=[X-\mu(z)]+[\mu(z)-a]. Expanding the squared norm gives \|X-a\|^2=\|X-\mu(z)\|^2+\|\mu(z)-a\|^2
+2[X-\mu(z)]^\top[\mu(z)-a]. 3 · Evaluate the cross term Given Z=z , the vector \mu(z)-a is fixed and \mathbb E[X-\mu(z)\mid Z=z]=0 . Thus the expected cross term is zero, and \mathbb E[\|X-a\|^2\mid z]=\mathbb E[\|X-\mu(z)\|^2\mid z]+\|\mu(z)-a\|^2. Only the last term depends on a , and it is minimized at a=\mu(z) . 4 · Read the consequence for a denoising model The population optimum is g^*(z)=\mathbb E[X\mid Z=z] . If corruption makes several clean inputs plausible, squared-error training averages them. A blurred reconstruction can therefore follow from ambiguity and the chosen loss, not only inadequate model capacity. 5 · State the limits of the result A finite neural network, finite training sample, or imperfect optimizer may not reach this optimum. The corruption distribution determines the conditional mean being learned. Denoising success does not alone certify anomaly detection, class separation, or a useful causal representation. Expanded derivation Chapter source · PDF p. 15 Link to this calculation ↗ Sparse and overcomplete codes A latent layer need not be small to be constrained. A sparse autoencoder can use many available units while penalizing frequent activation. The guide discusses a KL penalty on mean hidden activity. The constraint is on code usage rather than only on dimensionality. This is different from dropout’s random temporary masks and from an L1 penalty on network weights. Each acts on a different object in the learning system. Anomaly detection is conditional on reconstruction behavior The source proposes training primarily on normal data and scoring s(x)=\lVert x-\hat x\rVert^2 . A high score can flag observations that are poorly represented by the learned reconstruction system. The guide’s illustrative distributions of reconstruction error. Their overlap shows why a threshold involves a trade-off; the histogram is not a measured guarantee for a deployed detector. Architectures · PDF p. 16 The key assumption is that anomalous observations reconstruct substantially worse than normal observations. An overly expressive autoencoder can reconstruct anomalies too well, and normal distribution shifts can also raise scores. A threshold therefore needs validation and a connection to the relevant false-positive or downstream cost. Practical support without a second code library The official VAE example is linked as a related probabilistic extension , not mislabeled as a deterministic denoising tutorial. For the exact clean-target/corrupted-input distinction, the optional local companion provides a small synthetic denoising example with fixed validation corruption and held-out evaluation. It demonstrates that objective only; it does not claim that the toy results establish real anomaly-detection performance. The next chapter explains why adding a latent distribution and KL term changes an autoencoder into a different probabilistic construction.

The first term is constant. Minimizing error is equivalent to maximizing variance captured by the $k$-dimensional subspace.

#### 3 · Rotate into covariance eigenvectors
Write $S=V\Lambda V^\top$, with eigenvalues $\lambda_1\ge\cdots\ge\lambda_d\ge0$, and put $C=V^\top U$. Then $C^\top C=I$ and
$$\operatorname{tr}(U^\top SU)=\operatorname{tr}(C^\top\Lambda C)
=\sum_{i=1}^d\lambda_i\sum_{j=1}^k C_{ij}^2.$$
Let $a_i=\sum_jC_{ij}^2$. Because $CC^\top$ is an orthogonal projector, $0\le a_i\le1$ and $\sum_i a_i=k$.

#### 4 · Allocate captured dimensions to the largest eigenvalues
For ordered eigenvalues, the largest possible weighted sum under those constraints is $\sum_{i=1}^k\lambda_i$: if weight remains on a smaller eigenvalue while a larger one has available capacity, transferring that weight cannot reduce the sum. Choosing $U$ as the first $k$ eigenvectors attains this bound.
Thus the minimum reconstruction error is $\sum_{i=k+1}^d\lambda_i$.

#### 5 · Avoid claiming unique latent coordinates
For unconstrained linear encoder/decoder matrices, the principal reconstruction subspace can be represented in many latent bases. Replacing an encoder by $RE$ and decoder by $DR^{-1}$ for invertible $R$ leaves $DE$ unchanged. An ordinary nonlinear autoencoder therefore neither guarantees PCA coordinates nor solves this exact orthogonal projection problem. The equivalence concerns the optimal linear squared-error reconstruction subspace under appropriate conditions.

derivations.title: Derive the optimal denoising reconstruction under squared error
derivations.search:
**Setting.** Let clean data be a random vector $X$ and corrupted input be $Z$. Train a reconstruction function $g$ by minimizing $\mathbb E\|X-g(Z)\|^2$. Assume the relevant conditional second moments exist. The function class is unrestricted for this population argument.

#### 1 · Condition on a particular corrupted observation
At $Z=z$, a proposed reconstruction $a=g(z)$ incurs conditional risk $\mathbb E[\|X-a\|^2\mid Z=z]$. Define $\mu(z)=\mathbb E[X\mid Z=z]$.

#### 2 · Add and subtract the conditional mean
$$X-a=[X-\mu(z)]+[\mu(z)-a].$$
Expanding the squared norm gives
$$\|X-a\|^2=\|X-\mu(z)\|^2+\|\mu(z)-a\|^2
+2[X-\mu(z)]^\top[\mu(z)-a].$$

#### 3 · Evaluate the cross term
Given $Z=z$, the vector $\mu(z)-a$ is fixed and $\mathbb E[X-\mu(z)\mid Z=z]=0$. Thus the expected cross term is zero, and
$$\mathbb E[\|X-a\|^2\mid z]=\mathbb E[\|X-\mu(z)\|^2\mid z]+\|\mu(z)-a\|^2.$$
Only the last term depends on $a$, and it is minimized at $a=\mu(z)$.

#### 4 · Read the consequence for a denoising model
The population optimum is $g^*(z)=\mathbb E[X\mid Z=z]$. If corruption makes several clean inputs plausible, squared-error training averages them. A blurred reconstruction can therefore follow from ambiguity and the chosen loss, not only inadequate model capacity.

#### 5 · State the limits of the result
A finite neural network, finite training sample, or imperfect optimizer may not reach this optimum. The corruption distribution determines the conditional mean being learned. Denoising success does not alone certify anomaly detection, class separation, or a useful causal representation.

title: Variational autoencoders and the ELBO
summary: Derive the lower bound, interpret the two terms, and explain how reparameterization permits gradients.
search:
Replace a point code with a conditional distribution A deterministic autoencoder assigns a code to an input. A VAE encoder parameterizes an approximate posterior, commonly q_\phi(z\mid x)=\mathcal N\left(\mu_\phi(x),\operatorname{diag}(\sigma_\phi^2(x))\right). The latent prior is often p(z)=\mathcal N(0,I) , and a decoder specifies a likelihood p_\theta(x\mid z) . The goal is not merely to reconstruct one point through a noisy layer; it is to learn a latent-variable generative model with a tractable approximation to inference. The bound in the source The architecture guide gives \mathcal L_{\mathrm{ELBO}}(x)=\mathbb E_{q_\phi(z\mid x)}[\log p_\theta(x\mid z)]
-\operatorname{KL}(q_\phi(z\mid x)\Vert p(z)). Training minimizes the negative ELBO, equivalently maximizing this lower bound. The expectation rewards likelihood of the observed input under latent samples. The KL term pulls the approximate posterior toward the chosen prior. A “reconstruction loss” is therefore a negative log-likelihood term under a particular observation model, not an arbitrary interchangeable distance. The decoder’s output distribution determines what loss is consistent with it. Why it is a lower bound — expanded derivation The following fills in the algebra behind the source’s named bound. Introduce q_\phi(z\mid x) and rewrite \log p_\theta(x)=\mathcal L_{\mathrm{ELBO}}(x)+
\operatorname{KL}(q_\phi(z\mid x)\Vert p_\theta(z\mid x)). The last term is nonnegative, so the ELBO cannot exceed the log evidence. Equality holds when the approximate posterior matches the model posterior, subject to the usual distribution/support conditions. Expanding the ELBO expectation as \mathbb E_q[\log p_\theta(x,z)-\log q_\phi(z\mid x)] and using p_\theta(x,z)=p_\theta(x\mid z)p(z) gives the two terms displayed in the PDF. This separates the tractable training bound from the generally difficult exact posterior. Step by step Derive the evidence bound and identify its exact gap Setting. Fix an observed x with p_\theta(x)>0 . Let q_\phi(z\mid x) be a normalized density, with support compatible with the following ratios and finite expectations. All logarithms are natural. 1 · Introduce the latent variable and an auxiliary density Marginalization gives p_\theta(x)=\int p_\theta(x,z)\,dz . If q covers the relevant joint support, multiply and divide the integrand by q : p_\theta(x)=\int q_\phi(z\mid x)\frac{p_\theta(x,z)}{q_\phi(z\mid x)}\,dz
=\mathbb E_q\left[\frac{p_\theta(x,z)}{q_\phi(z\mid x)}\right]. 2 · Apply concavity of the logarithm For positive R , Jensen’s inequality says \log\mathbb E[R]\ge\mathbb E[\log R] . Therefore \log p_\theta(x)\ge\mathbb E_q[\log p_\theta(x,z)-\log q_\phi(z\mid x)]\equiv\mathcal E(\theta,\phi;x). This quantity \mathcal E is the evidence lower bound, or ELBO. 3 · Factor the joint model Use p_\theta(x,z)=p_\theta(x\mid z)p(z) . Logarithms split the product: \mathcal E=\mathbb E_q[\log p_\theta(x\mid z)]
+\mathbb E_q[\log p(z)-\log q_\phi(z\mid x)]. The second term is negative KL, yielding \mathcal E=\mathbb E_q[\log p_\theta(x\mid z)]-
D_{\mathrm{KL}}(q_\phi(z\mid x)\|p(z)). 4 · Derive the gap directly using Bayes’ rule Since p_\theta(z\mid x)=p_\theta(x,z)/p_\theta(x) , D_{\mathrm{KL}}(q\|p_\theta(z\mid x))
=\mathbb E_q[\log q-\log p_\theta(x,z)+\log p_\theta(x)]. The evidence is constant with respect to z , so this becomes D_{\mathrm{KL}}(q\|p_\theta(z\mid x))=\log p_\theta(x)-\mathcal E. Rearranging gives an exact identity, not merely an inequality. The KL-to- posterior is the gap; the KL-to- prior is the term appearing in the decomposed training bound. They are different objects. 5 · Justify nonnegativity For normalized compatible densities q,p , concavity gives \mathbb E_q\log\frac pq\le\log\mathbb E_q\frac pq\le\log1=0. Negating yields D_{\mathrm{KL}}(q\|p)\ge0 . Equality requires matching distributions almost everywhere. Thus the bound is tight exactly when the variational posterior matches the true posterior under the stated conditions. 6 · Convert the bound to a minimized objective Training typically minimizes -\mathcal E=\mathbb E_q[-\log p_\theta(x\mid z)]+D_{\mathrm{KL}}(q\|p(z)) . A changed coefficient on KL or an independently rescaled reconstruction loss changes this objective; it is not automatically the same model’s exact negative ELBO. The source instead writes \epsilon\sim\mathcal N(0,I),\qquad z=\mu_\phi(x)+\sigma_\phi(x)\odot\epsilon. The random draw now has a fixed parameter-independent distribution. For a sampled \epsilon , the transformation from \mu,\sigma to z is differentiable. A Monte Carlo estimate can then pass gradients through the decoder and into the encoder parameters. This does not eliminate sampling variation. It gives a usable gradient path for the selected distributional family. Step by step Differentiate through Gaussian reparameterization Setting. Draw \varepsilon\sim\mathcal N(0,I) independently of model parameters. Define z=\mu_\phi(x)+\sigma_\phi(x)\odot\varepsilon . Assume enough regularity to exchange differentiation and expectation. 1 · Verify the sample distribution Each coordinate has mean \mu_j+\sigma_j\mathbb E[\varepsilon_j]=\mu_j and variance \sigma_j^2\operatorname{Var}(\varepsilon_j)=\sigma_j^2 . Independent noise coordinates yield diagonal covariance, so this construction samples the desired Gaussian. 2 · Rewrite the expectation over fixed base noise For a differentiable function F , the equal distributions imply \mathbb E_{z\sim q_\phi}[F(z)]=\mathbb E_\varepsilon[F(\mu_\phi+\sigma_\phi\odot\varepsilon)]. The distribution on the right does not move when \phi changes; only the transformation does. 3 · Apply the chain rule to a sampled computation Let g_j=\partial F/\partial z_j . Holding the sampled \varepsilon fixed, \frac{\partial F}{\partial\mu_j}=g_j,\qquad
\frac{\partial F}{\partial\sigma_j}=g_j\varepsilon_j. If the network emits \ell_j=\log\sigma_j^2 , then \sigma_j=e^{\ell_j/2} and \frac{\partial\sigma_j}{\partial\ell_j}=\tfrac12e^{\ell_j/2}=\tfrac12\sigma_j, so \partial F/\partial\ell_j=g_j\varepsilon_j\sigma_j/2 . 4 · Continue to encoder parameters \nabla_\phi\mathbb E[F(z)]
=\mathbb E_\varepsilon\left[\sum_j g_j\left(\nabla_\phi\mu_j+\varepsilon_j\nabla_\phi\sigma_j\right)\right]. A sample average of the bracketed term estimates this gradient. If F also depends explicitly on \phi , its direct derivative must be added; the formula above assumes its parameter dependence is through z . 5 · Interpret the randomness correctly We do not differentiate the random-number generator. We differentiate a deterministic transformation of already sampled noise, then average over such computations. This is a pathwise gradient estimator; it does not by itself establish a valid pathwise estimator for discrete categorical sampling. This is an implementation supplement to the source’s general KL notation. If \mu=0 and every \sigma_j^2=1 , the divergence is zero. Moving a mean away from zero or changing the variances incurs a penalty. The code predicts a log variance and computes the standard deviation as \exp(\tfrac12\log\sigma^2) . Confusing variance with standard deviation changes the sampled distribution. The example also shows how the reconstruction and KL reductions are combined; their relative scale must remain intentional. Step by step Derive every term of the diagonal-Gaussian KL Setting. Let q(z\mid x)=\mathcal N(\mu,\operatorname{diag}(\sigma_1^2,\ldots,\sigma_d^2)) with every \sigma_j>0 , and let p(z)=\mathcal N(0,I) . The parameters are fixed for the observed x during this calculation. 1 · Write both log densities \log q(z)=-\frac d2\log(2\pi)-\sum_j\log\sigma_j
-\frac12\sum_j\frac{(z_j-\mu_j)^2}{\sigma_j^2}, \log p(z)=-\frac d2\log(2\pi)-\frac12\sum_jz_j^2. 2 · Subtract to cancel the normalization constants \log\frac{q(z)}{p(z)}
=\frac12\sum_j\left[z_j^2-\frac{(z_j-\mu_j)^2}{\sigma_j^2}-\log\sigma_j^2\right]. The logarithmic term uses 2\log\sigma_j=\log\sigma_j^2 . 3 · Evaluate each expectation under q By definition, \mathbb E_q[z_j]=\mu_j and \operatorname{Var}_q(z_j)=\sigma_j^2 . Hence \mathbb E_q[z_j^2]=\sigma_j^2+\mu_j^2,\qquad
\mathbb E_q[(z_j-\mu_j)^2/\sigma_j^2]=1. The log variance is constant under this expectation. 4 · Substitute and sum D_{\mathrm{KL}}(q\|p)=\frac12\sum_{j=1}^d
\left(\mu_j^2+\sigma_j^2-1-\log\sigma_j^2\right). For network output \ell_j=\log\sigma_j^2 , substitute \sigma_j^2=e^{\ell_j} : D_{\mathrm{KL}}=\frac12\sum_j(\mu_j^2+e^{\ell_j}-1-\ell_j). Each term is nonnegative because u-1-\log u\ge0 for u>0 and \mu_j^2\ge0 . 5 · Differentiate the analytic result \frac{\partial D_{\mathrm{KL}}}{\partial\mu_j}=\mu_j,\qquad
\frac{\partial D_{\mathrm{KL}}}{\partial\ell_j}=\frac12(e^{\ell_j}-1). For \mu=0 and \ell=0 , the posterior equals the prior, so KL and both derivatives vanish. A batch objective may average these per-example values, while its reconstruction likelihood normally sums observed dimensions per example. Averaging one term over its dimensions but not the other changes their relative weight. If the latent variable is ignored, a low KL by itself is not evidence of a useful representation. If reconstruction dominates without an appropriate prior relationship, the generative interpretation can weaken. The supplied guide introduces the VAE rather than providing a full catalogue of its training pathologies. The linked official implementation supplies training, sampling, and reconstruction images. Those existing visualizations make a separate local VAE training script unnecessary here.

derivations.title: Derive the evidence bound and identify its exact gap
derivations.search:
**Setting.** Fix an observed $x$ with $p_\theta(x)>0$. Let $q_\phi(z\mid x)$ be a normalized density, with support compatible with the following ratios and finite expectations. All logarithms are natural.

#### 1 · Introduce the latent variable and an auxiliary density
Marginalization gives $p_\theta(x)=\int p_\theta(x,z)\,dz$. If $q$ covers the relevant joint support, multiply and divide the integrand by $q$:
$$p_\theta(x)=\int q_\phi(z\mid x)\frac{p_\theta(x,z)}{q_\phi(z\mid x)}\,dz
=\mathbb E_q\left[\frac{p_\theta(x,z)}{q_\phi(z\mid x)}\right].$$

#### 2 · Apply concavity of the logarithm
For positive $R$, Jensen’s inequality says $\log\mathbb E[R]\ge\mathbb E[\log R]$. Therefore
$$\log p_\theta(x)\ge\mathbb E_q[\log p_\theta(x,z)-\log q_\phi(z\mid x)]\equiv\mathcal E(\theta,\phi;x).$$
This quantity $\mathcal E$ is the evidence lower bound, or ELBO.

#### 3 · Factor the joint model
Use $p_\theta(x,z)=p_\theta(x\mid z)p(z)$. Logarithms split the product:
$$\mathcal E=\mathbb E_q[\log p_\theta(x\mid z)]
+\mathbb E_q[\log p(z)-\log q_\phi(z\mid x)].$$
The second term is negative KL, yielding
$$\mathcal E=\mathbb E_q[\log p_\theta(x\mid z)]-
D_{\rm KL}(q_\phi(z\mid x)\|p(z)).$$

#### 4 · Derive the gap directly using Bayes’ rule
Since $p_\theta(z\mid x)=p_\theta(x,z)/p_\theta(x)$,
$$D_{\rm KL}(q\|p_\theta(z\mid x))
=\mathbb E_q[\log q-\log p_\theta(x,z)+\log p_\theta(x)].$$
The evidence is constant with respect to $z$, so this becomes
$$D_{\rm KL}(q\|p_\theta(z\mid x))=\log p_\theta(x)-\mathcal E.$$
Rearranging gives an exact identity, not merely an inequality. The KL-to-**posterior** is the gap; the KL-to-**prior** is the term appearing in the decomposed training bound. They are different objects.

#### 5 · Justify nonnegativity
For normalized compatible densities $q,p$, concavity gives
$$\mathbb E_q\log\frac pq\le\log\mathbb E_q\frac pq\le\log1=0.$$
Negating yields $D_{\rm KL}(q\|p)\ge0$. Equality requires matching distributions almost everywhere. Thus the bound is tight exactly when the variational posterior matches the true posterior under the stated conditions.

#### 6 · Convert the bound to a minimized objective
Training typically minimizes $-\mathcal E=\mathbb E_q[-\log p_\theta(x\mid z)]+D_{\rm KL}(q\|p(z))$. A changed coefficient on KL or an independently rescaled reconstruction loss changes this objective; it is not automatically the same model’s exact negative ELBO.

derivations.title: Derive every term of the diagonal-Gaussian KL
derivations.search:
**Setting.** Let $q(z\mid x)=\mathcal N(\mu,\operatorname{diag}(\sigma_1^2,\ldots,\sigma_d^2))$ with every $\sigma_j>0$, and let $p(z)=\mathcal N(0,I)$. The parameters are fixed for the observed $x$ during this calculation.

#### 1 · Write both log densities
$$\log q(z)=-\frac d2\log(2\pi)-\sum_j\log\sigma_j
-\frac12\sum_j\frac{(z_j-\mu_j)^2}{\sigma_j^2},$$
$$\log p(z)=-\frac d2\log(2\pi)-\frac12\sum_jz_j^2.$$

#### 2 · Subtract to cancel the normalization constants
$$\log\frac{q(z)}{p(z)}
=\frac12\sum_j\left[z_j^2-\frac{(z_j-\mu_j)^2}{\sigma_j^2}-\log\sigma_j^2\right].$$
The logarithmic term uses $2\log\sigma_j=\log\sigma_j^2$.

#### 3 · Evaluate each expectation under q
By definition, $\mathbb E_q[z_j]=\mu_j$ and $\operatorname{Var}_q(z_j)=\sigma_j^2$. Hence
$$\mathbb E_q[z_j^2]=\sigma_j^2+\mu_j^2,\qquad
\mathbb E_q[(z_j-\mu_j)^2/\sigma_j^2]=1.$$
The log variance is constant under this expectation.

#### 4 · Substitute and sum
$$D_{\rm KL}(q\|p)=\frac12\sum_{j=1}^d
\left(\mu_j^2+\sigma_j^2-1-\log\sigma_j^2\right).$$
For network output $\ell_j=\log\sigma_j^2$, substitute $\sigma_j^2=e^{\ell_j}$:
$$D_{\rm KL}=\frac12\sum_j(\mu_j^2+e^{\ell_j}-1-\ell_j).$$
Each term is nonnegative because $u-1-\log u\ge0$ for $u>0$ and $\mu_j^2\ge0$.

#### 5 · Differentiate the analytic result
$$\frac{\partial D_{\rm KL}}{\partial\mu_j}=\mu_j,\qquad
\frac{\partial D_{\rm KL}}{\partial\ell_j}=\frac12(e^{\ell_j}-1).$$
For $\mu=0$ and $\ell=0$, the posterior equals the prior, so KL and both derivatives vanish. With $\mu=1,\sigma=2$, one dimension contributes $(1+4-1-\log4)/2\approx1.30685$.

#### 6 · Keep the reduction consistent
The displayed expression sums latent coordinates for one example. A batch objective may average these per-example values, while its reconstruction likelihood normally sums observed dimensions per example. Averaging one term over its dimensions but not the other changes their relative weight.

**Setting.** Draw $\varepsilon\sim\mathcal N(0,I)$ independently of model parameters. Define $z=\mu_\phi(x)+\sigma_\phi(x)\odot\varepsilon$. Assume enough regularity to exchange differentiation and expectation.

$$\mathbb E_{z\sim q_\phi}[F(z)]=\mathbb E_\varepsilon[F(\mu_\phi+\sigma_\phi\odot\varepsilon)].$$
The distribution on the right does not move when $\phi$ changes; only the transformation does.

#### 3 · Apply the chain rule to a sampled computation
Let $g_j=\partial F/\partial z_j$. Holding the sampled $\varepsilon$ fixed,
$$\frac{\partial F}{\partial\mu_j}=g_j,\qquad
\frac{\partial F}{\partial\sigma_j}=g_j\varepsilon_j.$$
If the network emits $\ell_j=\log\sigma_j^2$, then $\sigma_j=e^{\ell_j/2}$ and
$$\frac{\partial\sigma_j}{\partial\ell_j}=\tfrac12e^{\ell_j/2}=\tfrac12\sigma_j,$$
so $\partial F/\partial\ell_j=g_j\varepsilon_j\sigma_j/2$.

#### 4 · Continue to encoder parameters
$$\nabla_\phi\mathbb E[F(z)]

title: Attention: queries, keys, values, and weights
summary: Derive the routing calculation and follow the guide’s numerical weighted mixture.
search:
Attention is content-dependent retrieval A query retrieves a weighted combination of values. Keys determine how strongly each source matches that query. The three roles are distinct even when all are projected from the same input sequence. For X\in\mathbb R^{T\times d_{\mathrm{model}}} , the source forms Q=XW_Q , K=XW_K , and V=XW_V . Scaled dot-product attention is \operatorname{Attention}(Q,K,V)=
\operatorname{softmax}\left(\frac{QK^\top}{\sqrt{d_k}}\right)V. Softmax is applied across the allowed keys for each query row. The output is a mixture of values , not a mixture of keys. The score matrix determines where to retrieve; the value matrix determines what is retrieved. Shapes explain the operation If Q has T_q rows and K,V have T_k rows, then QK^\top has shape T_q\times T_k . Each query receives one score for each key. Multiplying the normalized scores by V\in\mathbb R^{T_k\times d_v} produces T_q\times d_v outputs. This is an expanded shape reading of the source equation. Query count and key count need not match, which is important for cross-attention between different sequences. Step by step Derive attention gradients with respect to queries, keys, and values Setting. For one head, let Q\in\mathbb R^{T\times d_k} , K\in\mathbb R^{S\times d_k} , V\in\mathbb R^{S\times d_v} . Define A=QK^\top/\sqrt{d_k} , rowwise probabilities P=\operatorname{softmax}(A) , and O=PV . Assume each row has at least one allowed key. Hold any mask fixed and ignore dropout for this derivation. Let incoming gradient G=\partial L/\partial O have shape T\times d_v . 1 · Differentiate the value mixture entry by entry O_{ib}=\sum_{j=1}^SP_{ij}V_{jb}. Thus the gradient with respect to one value element is \sum_iG_{ib}P_{ij} , and the gradient with respect to one probability is \sum_bG_{ib}V_{jb} . In matrix form, \bar V=P^\top G,\qquad \bar P=GV^\top. Their shapes are S\times d_v and T\times S . 2 · Apply the full rowwise softmax Jacobian For fixed query row i , \partial P_{ij}/\partial A_{ir}=P_{ij}(\mathbf1_{j=r}-P_{ir}) . Sum over all affected outputs in that row: \bar A_{ir}=\sum_j\bar P_{ij}P_{ij}(\mathbf1_{j=r}-P_{ir})
=P_{ir}\left[\bar P_{ir}-\sum_jP_{ij}\bar P_{ij}\right]. The bracket subtracts a probability-weighted row mean. This avoids constructing a dense S\times S Jacobian for each row. 3 · Differentiate the scaled scores A_{ij}=\frac1{\sqrt{d_k}}\sum_aQ_{ia}K_{ja}. Hence \bar Q_{ia}=\frac1{\sqrt{d_k}}\sum_j\bar A_{ij}K_{ja},\qquad
\bar K_{ja}=\frac1{\sqrt{d_k}}\sum_i\bar A_{ij}Q_{ia}. Collecting entries gives \bar Q=\frac{\bar AK}{\sqrt{d_k}},\qquad
\bar K=\frac{\bar A^\top Q}{\sqrt{d_k}}. 4 · Continue through shared self-attention inputs If Q=XW_Q , K=XW_K , and V=XW_V , then \bar X=\bar QW_Q^\top+\bar KW_K^\top+\bar VW_V^\top, \bar W_Q=X^\top\bar Q,\quad\bar W_K=X^\top\bar K,\quad\bar W_V=X^\top\bar V. All three branches depend on X , so their contributions must be added. Cross-attention has different query and key/value source tensors, so their gradient branches are accumulated to the appropriate source instead. 5 · Respect operations omitted from the derivation Attention dropout, output projection, residual paths, and normalization contribute additional local derivatives when present. Masked positions have no score influence when their probability is fixed at zero. This derivation verifies the elementary attention operation, not every optimized kernel or complete Transformer block. Expanded derivation Chapter source · PDF p. 18 Link to this calculation ↗ Why the square-root scale appears For the initialization-scale argument, assume independent, zero-mean query/key components with unit variance and no cross-coordinate dependence. Summing d_k products gives a dot-product variance growing with d_k . Large logits can make softmax highly concentrated and reduce useful sensitivity. Dividing by \sqrt{d_k} controls this dimension-induced scale. The assumption explains the design choice; it does not say that every trained query/key distribution is exactly independent or unit variance. Learned projections, normalization, and actual data affect the observed scores. Step by step Derive the square-root attention scale from moments Setting. Let s=q^\top k=\sum_{j=1}^{d_k}q_jk_j . For this initialization-scale argument, assume pairs across coordinates are independent; within each pair, q_j and k_j are independent, zero mean, and have variances v_q and v_k . Real learned queries and keys need not retain these assumptions. 1 · Evaluate one product’s mean Independence gives \mathbb E[q_jk_j]=\mathbb E[q_j]\mathbb E[k_j]=0 . 2 · Evaluate its second moment and variance \mathbb E[(q_jk_j)^2]=\mathbb E[q_j^2]\mathbb E[k_j^2]=v_qv_k. Since the mean is zero, this is also \operatorname{Var}(q_jk_j) . 3 · Sum the coordinate contributions \operatorname{Var}(s)=\sum_j\operatorname{Var}(q_jk_j)
+\sum_{j\ne r}\operatorname{Cov}(q_jk_j,q_rk_r). Coordinate independence makes the covariance terms zero. Therefore \operatorname{Var}(s)=d_kv_qv_k . 4 · Scale the standard deviation, not the variance directly For a=s/\sqrt{d_k} , variance scales by the square of the divisor: \operatorname{Var}(a)=\frac{\operatorname{Var}(s)}{d_k}=v_qv_k. With unit component variances, the scaled score has variance one. Dividing by d_k would instead make its variance 1/d_k . 5 · Connect score scale to softmax sensitivity For weights p_i=\operatorname{softmax}(s)_i , the derivative is \partial p_i/\partial s_j=p_i(\mathbf1_{i=j}-p_j) . When one score dominates and the distribution saturates, many of these derivatives approach zero. Scaling avoids a predictable increase in score magnitude with width under the stated assumptions. It is not a proof that all trained scores have unit variance or that saturation can never occur. With d_k=2 , scaled scores are approximately (0.707,0,0.707) , giving weights \alpha\approx(0.401,0.198,0.401). For values v_1=(1,0) , v_2=(0,2) , and v_3=(1,1) , \alpha_1v_1+\alpha_2v_2+\alpha_3v_3\approx(0.802,0.797). The second source has a lower weight but still contributes to the second output coordinate because its value has magnitude two there. A large attention coefficient alone is not a full measure of a source’s eventual effect on a prediction. The source’s illustrative self-attention matrix. Rows describe query-specific distributions over keys. These are illustrative weights, not measurements from a trained language model. Architectures · PDF p. 19 Step by step Calculate scores, normalization, and the value mixture Setting. Use the supplied query q=(1,0) , keys k_1=(1,0) , k_2=(0,1) , k_3=(1,1) , and values v_1=(1,0) , v_2=(0,2) , v_3=(1,1) . derivations.title: Derive the square-root attention scale from moments
derivations.search:
**Setting.** Let $s=q^\top k=\sum_{j=1}^{d_k}q_jk_j$. For this initialization-scale argument, assume pairs across coordinates are independent; within each pair, $q_j$ and $k_j$ are independent, zero mean, and have variances $v_q$ and $v_k$. Real learned queries and keys need not retain these assumptions.

#### 1 · Evaluate one product’s mean
Independence gives $\mathbb E[q_jk_j]=\mathbb E[q_j]\mathbb E[k_j]=0$.

#### 2 · Evaluate its second moment and variance
$$\mathbb E[(q_jk_j)^2]=\mathbb E[q_j^2]\mathbb E[k_j^2]=v_qv_k.$$
Since the mean is zero, this is also $\operatorname{Var}(q_jk_j)$.

#### 3 · Sum the coordinate contributions
$$\operatorname{Var}(s)=\sum_j\operatorname{Var}(q_jk_j)
+\sum_{j\ne r}\operatorname{Cov}(q_jk_j,q_rk_r).$$
Coordinate independence makes the covariance terms zero. Therefore $\operatorname{Var}(s)=d_kv_qv_k$.

#### 4 · Scale the standard deviation, not the variance directly
For $a=s/\sqrt{d_k}$, variance scales by the square of the divisor:
$$\operatorname{Var}(a)=\frac{\operatorname{Var}(s)}{d_k}=v_qv_k.$$
With unit component variances, the scaled score has variance one. Dividing by $d_k$ would instead make its variance $1/d_k$.

#### 5 · Connect score scale to softmax sensitivity
For weights $p_i=\operatorname{softmax}(s)_i$, the derivative is $\partial p_i/\partial s_j=p_i(\mathbf1_{i=j}-p_j)$. When one score dominates and the distribution saturates, many of these derivatives approach zero. Scaling avoids a predictable increase in score magnitude with width under the stated assumptions. It is not a proof that all trained scores have unit variance or that saturation can never occur.

derivations.title: Calculate scores, normalization, and the value mixture
derivations.search:
**Setting.** Use the supplied query $q=(1,0)$, keys $k_1=(1,0)$, $k_2=(0,1)$, $k_3=(1,1)$, and values $v_1=(1,0)$, $v_2=(0,2)$, $v_3=(1,1)$. The key width is $d_k=2$.

#### 1 · Form every dot product
$$q^\top k_1=1(1)+0(0)=1,\quad q^\top k_2=1(0)+0(1)=0,$$
$$q^\top k_3=1(1)+0(1)=1.$$
Dividing by $\sqrt2$ gives scores $(1/\sqrt2,0,1/\sqrt2)$.

#### 2 · Shift the scores before exponentiating
Subtract their maximum $1/\sqrt2$, which leaves softmax unchanged. The shifted exponentials are
$$(1,e^{-1/\sqrt2},1)\approx(1,0.4930687,1).$$
Their sum is approximately $2.4930687$.

#### 3 · Normalize each value
$$\alpha_1=\alpha_3=\frac1{2+e^{-1/\sqrt2}}\approx0.4011121,$$
$$\alpha_2=\frac{e^{-1/\sqrt2}}{2+e^{-1/\sqrt2}}\approx0.1977758.$$
The weights are positive and sum to one by construction.

#### 4 · Compute each output coordinate
$$o_1=\alpha_1(1)+\alpha_2(0)+\alpha_3(1)=\alpha_1+\alpha_3\approx0.8022242,$$
$$o_2=\alpha_1(0)+\alpha_2(2)+\alpha_3(1)=2\alpha_2+\alpha_3\approx0.7966637.$$
Keys determine the weights; values supply the vectors being mixed. A key and its corresponding value do not have to be equal vectors.

#### 5 · Handle a mask before normalization
A disallowed position receives score $-\infty$ and exponential zero. Normalize only over the remaining allowed positions. If **all** positions are disallowed, the mathematical denominator is zero and no probability distribution is defined by this formula; prevent that case or handle it explicitly according to the chosen implementation.

derivations.title: Derive attention gradients with respect to queries, keys, and values
derivations.search:
**Setting.** For one head, let $Q\in\mathbb R^{T\times d_k}$, $K\in\mathbb R^{S\times d_k}$, $V\in\mathbb R^{S\times d_v}$. Define $A=QK^\top/\sqrt{d_k}$, rowwise probabilities $P=\operatorname{softmax}(A)$, and $O=PV$. Assume each row has at least one allowed key. Hold any mask fixed and ignore dropout for this derivation. Let incoming gradient $G=\partial L/\partial O$ have shape $T\times d_v$.

#### 1 · Differentiate the value mixture entry by entry
$$O_{ib}=\sum_{j=1}^SP_{ij}V_{jb}.$$
Thus the gradient with respect to one value element is $\sum_iG_{ib}P_{ij}$, and the gradient with respect to one probability is $\sum_bG_{ib}V_{jb}$. In matrix form,
$$\bar V=P^\top G,\qquad \bar P=GV^\top.$$
Their shapes are $S\times d_v$ and $T\times S$.

#### 2 · Apply the full rowwise softmax Jacobian
For fixed query row $i$, $\partial P_{ij}/\partial A_{ir}=P_{ij}(\mathbf1_{j=r}-P_{ir})$. Sum over all affected outputs in that row:
$$\bar A_{ir}=\sum_j\bar P_{ij}P_{ij}(\mathbf1_{j=r}-P_{ir})
=P_{ir}\left[\bar P_{ir}-\sum_jP_{ij}\bar P_{ij}\right].$$
The bracket subtracts a probability-weighted row mean. This avoids constructing a dense $S\times S$ Jacobian for each row.

#### 3 · Differentiate the scaled scores
$$A_{ij}=\frac1{\sqrt{d_k}}\sum_aQ_{ia}K_{ja}.$$
Hence
$$\bar Q_{ia}=\frac1{\sqrt{d_k}}\sum_j\bar A_{ij}K_{ja},\qquad
\bar K_{ja}=\frac1{\sqrt{d_k}}\sum_i\bar A_{ij}Q_{ia}.$$
Collecting entries gives
$$\bar Q=\frac{\bar AK}{\sqrt{d_k}},\qquad
\bar K=\frac{\bar A^\top Q}{\sqrt{d_k}}.$$

#### 4 · Continue through shared self-attention inputs
If $Q=XW_Q$, $K=XW_K$, and $V=XW_V$, then
$$\bar X=\bar QW_Q^\top+\bar KW_K^\top+\bar VW_V^\top,$$
$$\bar W_Q=X^\top\bar Q,\quad\bar W_K=X^\top\bar K,\quad\bar W_V=X^\top\bar V.$$
All three branches depend on $X$, so their contributions must be added. Cross-attention has different query and key/value source tensors, so their gradient branches are accumulated to the appropriate source instead.

#### 5 · Respect operations omitted from the derivation
Attention dropout, output projection, residual paths, and normalization contribute additional local derivatives when present. Masked positions have no score influence when their probability is fixed at zero. This derivation verifies the elementary attention operation, not every optimized kernel or complete Transformer block.

title: Transformers: position, residual paths, and masking
summary: Build the full architecture around attention and distinguish parallel training from sequential generation.

derivations.title: Prove attention equivariance and derive a sinusoidal position shift
derivations.search:
**Setting.** First consider self-attention without positional features, a fixed order-dependent mask, or stochastic dropout. Let $P$ be a permutation matrix, so $P^\top P=I$ and $PX$ reorders token rows.

#### 1 · Follow the permutation through the projections
For input $X'=PX$, shared linear projections give $Q'=PXW_Q=PQ$, $K'=PK$, and $V'=PV$. Thus the score matrix transforms as
$$A'=\frac{Q'K'^\top}{\sqrt{d_k}}=\frac{PQK^\top P^\top}{\sqrt{d_k}}=PAP^\top.$$

#### 2 · Follow it through rowwise normalization
Permuting a row’s entries permutes its exponentials but does not change their sum. Permuting rows simply reorders which row is normalized. Therefore
$$\operatorname{softmax}_{\rm row}(PAP^\top)=P\operatorname{softmax}_{\rm row}(A)P^\top.$$

#### 3 · Complete the attention operation
Writing $S=\operatorname{softmax}_{\rm row}(A)$,
$$O'=PSP^\top PV=PSV=PO.$$
The output permutes in the same way as the input: **equivariance**, not invariance. A shared per-token feed-forward function preserves this property; a symmetric pooling over tokens can turn it into invariance for a global prediction.

#### 4 · Identify what breaks the premise
A fixed triangular causal mask is not generally unchanged by an arbitrary permutation, so the preceding unrestricted-attention symmetry proof does not apply to that fixed-mask computation. Position embeddings, relative-position biases, recurrence, or masking can all supply order-dependent structure. Positional encoding is a common mechanism, not the only possible one.

#### 5 · Derive how one sinusoidal pair changes with position
For frequency $\omega$, define $v(p)=(\sin(\omega p),\cos(\omega p))^\top$. Angle addition gives
$$\sin[\omega(p+k)]=\sin(\omega p)\cos(\omega k)+\cos(\omega p)\sin(\omega k),$$
$$\cos[\omega(p+k)]=\cos(\omega p)\cos(\omega k)-\sin(\omega p)\sin(\omega k).$$
Consequently
$$v(p+k)=
\begin{bmatrix}\cos(\omega k)&\sin(\omega k)\\-\sin(\omega k)&\cos(\omega k)\end{bmatrix}v(p).$$
For a fixed offset $k$, this is the same linear transformation at every $p$. Using multiple frequencies gives several position scales. This algebra explains structure available to the model; it does not guarantee that a trained model extrapolates correctly to longer sequences.

derivations.title: Derive LayerNorm’s statistics and complete input gradient
derivations.search:
**Setting.** Normalize one token’s $d$ features $x_1,\ldots,x_d$. Let
$$\mu=\frac1d\sum_i x_i,\quad v=\frac1d\sum_i(x_i-\mu)^2,\quad
r=(v+\epsilon)^{-1/2},\quad\hat x_i=(x_i-\mu)r,$$
$$y_i=\gamma_i\hat x_i+\beta_i,\qquad\epsilon>0.$$
This uses the population-form divisor $d$, not $d-1$. The learned $\gamma,\beta$ do not depend on the token’s computed statistics.

#### 1 · Differentiate the mean
For every input coordinate $x_j$, $\partial\mu/\partial x_j=1/d$. Consequently,
$$\frac{\partial(x_i-\mu)}{\partial x_j}=\mathbf1_{i=j}-\frac1d.$$

#### 2 · Differentiate the variance, including the mean’s dependence
Apply the chain rule:
$$\frac{\partial v}{\partial x_j}=\frac2d\sum_i(x_i-\mu)\left(\mathbf1_{i=j}-\frac1d\right).$$
Because $\sum_i(x_i-\mu)=\sum_i x_i-d\mu=0$, the mean-related sum vanishes and
$$\frac{\partial v}{\partial x_j}=\frac2d(x_j-\mu).$$

#### 3 · Differentiate inverse standard deviation
$$\frac{\partial r}{\partial x_j}
=-\frac12(v+\epsilon)^{-3/2}\frac2d(x_j-\mu)
=-\frac{r^3}{d}(x_j-\mu).$$

#### 4 · Apply the product rule to the normalized feature
$$\frac{\partial\hat x_i}{\partial x_j}
=r\left(\mathbf1_{i=j}-\frac1d\right)-\frac{r^3}{d}(x_i-\mu)(x_j-\mu).$$
Using $(x_i-\mu)r=\hat x_i$, this becomes
$$\frac{\partial\hat x_i}{\partial x_j}
=r\left(\mathbf1_{i=j}-\frac1d-\frac{\hat x_i\hat x_j}{d}\right).$$
The formula retains $\epsilon$ through $r$ and the normalized features; it does not assume their variance is exactly one.

#### 5 · Contract the Jacobian with the upstream gradient
Let $g_i=\partial L/\partial y_i$ and $a_i=g_i\gamma_i$. Then
$$\frac{\partial L}{\partial x_j}
=\sum_i a_i\frac{\partial\hat x_i}{\partial x_j}
=r\left[a_j-\frac1d\sum_i a_i-\frac{\hat x_j}{d}\sum_i a_i\hat x_i\right].$$
The affine gradients are $\partial L/\partial\gamma_i=g_i\hat x_i$ and $\partial L/\partial\beta_i=g_i$, summed over examples or positions sharing these parameters.

#### 6 · Compare the normalized axes, not just the names
LayerNorm typically normalizes features within each token and uses those input statistics in both training and evaluation. Training BatchNorm normalizes across batch-related axes, so a prediction and its derivatives can depend on other batch members. They are not interchangeable operations merely because both subtract a mean and divide by a scale.

derivations.title: Derive residual-path gradients and compare pre-norm with post-norm
derivations.search:
**Setting.** For a residual transformation $y=x+F(x)$, let $J_F=\partial F/\partial x$. Treat vectors as columns and assume differentiability at the point considered.

#### 1 · Differentiate both additive branches
The identity branch has Jacobian $I$. Addition sums the contributions:
$$\frac{\partial y}{\partial x}=I+J_F.$$
For upstream loss gradient $g_y$, the chain rule gives
$$g_x=(I+J_F)^\top g_y=g_y+J_F^\top g_y.$$
The gradient therefore has a direct path that does not traverse $F$.

#### 2 · Expand two residual blocks
If $x_1=x_0+F_0(x_0)$ and $x_2=x_1+F_1(x_1)$, then
$$\frac{\partial x_2}{\partial x_0}=(I+J_{F_1})(I+J_{F_0})
=I+J_{F_0}+J_{F_1}+J_{F_1}J_{F_0}.$$
The identity term is one available path among several. The other terms can cancel or amplify it; residual connections do not prove the total gradient norm is bounded away from zero.

#### 3 · Include normalization before the sublayer
For pre-norm $y=x+F(N(x))$,
$$\frac{\partial y}{\partial x}=I+J_F(N(x))J_N(x).$$
The direct identity path remains outside normalization.

#### 4 · Include normalization after the residual sum
For post-norm $y=N(x+F(x))$,
$$\frac{\partial y}{\partial x}=J_N(x+F(x))(I+J_F(x)).$$
Now every path crosses the normalization Jacobian after the sum. These are distinct computations, even though both contain the same three ingredients.

#### 5 · Avoid a universal architecture verdict
This path analysis explains an optimization difference, not a theorem that one layout always wins. Initial scale, depth, initialization, normalization parameters, and optimizer settings affect the complete system. A final normalization after a stack also contributes its own Jacobian.

derivations.title: Count tensor elements, matrix products, and projection parameters
derivations.search:
**Setting.** Use batch $B=16$, length $T=100$, model width $d=256$, and $H=8$ heads. Split widths evenly so $d_k=d_v=d/H=32$. Ignore padding and describe an ordinary dense attention implementation.

#### 1 · Follow each shape
The model representation is $(B,T,d)=(16,100,256)$. Each head uses $Q_h,K_h,V_h$ with shape $(16,100,32)$. Multiplying $Q_hK_h^\top$ gives $(16,100,100)$ scores. Across heads, the score count is
$$BHT^2=16\cdot8\cdot100\cdot100=1{,}280{,}000.$$
At four bytes per scalar, one such tensor alone occupies $5{,}120{,}000$ bytes, before gradients, probabilities, or other activations.

#### 2 · Count pairwise arithmetic
For one head, computing $Q_hK_h^\top$ needs $BT^2d_k$ multiply–accumulate terms. Summing over heads gives $BT^2Hd_k=BT^2d$. Multiplying attention weights by values gives another $BT^2d$ term. This is the origin of the $O(BT^2d)$ interaction cost.

#### 3 · Include the projections that the interaction shorthand omits
Each of the three input projections maps $d$ to $d$ for every token, costing $BTd^2$ terms. The output projection adds one more, for roughly $4BTd^2$ projection terms. Thus full attention arithmetic includes both $BTd^2$ and $BT^2d$ contributions, before the feed-forward sublayer.

#### 4 · Count trainable parameters separately
Three dense $d\times d$ input projections plus one output projection have $4d^2$ weights. With one bias per projected feature in each map, add $4d$ biases. For $d=256$, that is $262{,}144+1{,}024=263{,}168$ parameters. This count does not multiply by $T$, $B$, or $H$ when total projected width remains $d$.

#### 5 · Distinguish arithmetic from materialized memory
A straightforward implementation stores the quadratic score/probability arrays. Memory-efficient fused attention can avoid materializing the complete matrices while computing equivalent dense attention, so the naive storage count is not a lower bound for every implementation. The quadratic all-pairs interaction arithmetic remains distinct from this memory optimization. Actual runtime also depends on kernels, hardware, masks, and sequence lengths.

title: GNNs, graph attention, and relational bottlenecks
summary: Explain message passing, permutation symmetry, normalization, and why learned edge weights do not remove every graph limitation.
search:
The input includes relationships A graph G=(V,E) specifies entities and their relations. Node neighborhoods can vary in size, and the arbitrary ordering of nodes in a file should not change what a model means. A graph network therefore needs a rule for combining variable-size neighborhoods with appropriate permutation symmetry. The source’s message-passing template is m_i^{(\ell)}=\operatorname{AGG}_{j\in\mathcal N(i)}
\psi_\ell(h_i^{(\ell)},h_j^{(\ell)},e_{ij}), h_i^{(\ell+1)}=\phi_\ell(h_i^{(\ell)},m_i^{(\ell)}). A symmetric sum, mean, or max aggregator does not depend on the order in which neighbors are listed. Shared update functions then produce node outputs that reorder consistently when the nodes are permuted. Normalized graph convolution The guide gives a common GCN propagation rule: \tilde A=A+I,\qquad\tilde D_{ii}=\sum_j\tilde A_{ij}, H^{(\ell+1)}=\sigma\left(\tilde D^{-1/2}\tilde A\tilde D^{-1/2}H^{(\ell)}W^{(\ell)}\right). Self-loops include a node’s own representation. Degree normalization controls scale so high-degree neighborhoods do not dominate merely by size. The learned transformation and nonlinear activation then produce the next representation. The source’s simple mean example is deliberately not the full symmetric-normalization formula: with scalar features 2,1,4 , node one averages itself and both neighbors to 7/3 . Multiplying by 0.5 and applying ReLU gives about 1.17 . A second node connected only to node one averages to 1.5 and updates to 0.75 . The example isolates the information-mixing idea. Step by step Calculate symmetric graph normalization, not just a neighbor mean Setting. Use an undirected three-node path 1\!-
obreakdash 2\!-
obreakdash 3 with no initial self-loops. Each node has scalar feature x=(2,1,4)^\top . We will add one self-loop per node and use a scalar feature weight w=0.5 followed by ReLU. 1 · Write adjacency and add self-loops A=\begin{bmatrix}0&1&0\\1&0&1\\0&1&0\end{bmatrix},\qquad
\tilde A=A+I=\begin{bmatrix}1&1&0\\1&1&1\\0&1&1\end{bmatrix}. Summing each row gives degrees \tilde d=(2,3,2) , so \tilde D^{-1/2}=\operatorname{diag}(1/\sqrt2,1/\sqrt3,1/\sqrt2) . 2 · Multiply the diagonal factors into each edge For S=\tilde D^{-1/2}\tilde A\tilde D^{-1/2} , entry (i,j) is \tilde A_{ij}/\sqrt{\tilde d_i\tilde d_j} . Hence S=\begin{bmatrix}
1/2&1/\sqrt6&0\\
1/\sqrt6&1/3&1/\sqrt6\\
0&1/\sqrt6&1/2
\end{bmatrix}. This matrix is symmetric, but its rows do not generally sum to one. 3 · Aggregate the features explicitly m_1=\tfrac12(2)+\tfrac1{\sqrt6}(1)=1+\tfrac1{\sqrt6}\approx1.408248, m_2=\tfrac1{\sqrt6}(2)+\tfrac13(1)+\tfrac1{\sqrt6}(4)
=\tfrac6{\sqrt6}+\tfrac13\approx2.782823, m_3=\tfrac1{\sqrt6}(1)+\tfrac12(4)=\tfrac1{\sqrt6}+2\approx2.408248. These are not the ordinary rowwise means (1.5,7/3,2.5) . 4 · Apply the learned feature transformation and activation h'=\operatorname{ReLU}(0.5m)\approx(0.704124,1.391412,1.204124)^\top. All components are positive in this example. With multiple features, H W transforms feature coordinates while S mixes node coordinates; their roles differ. 5 · State the graph assumptions This symmetric construction has its usual spectral interpretation for an undirected graph with nonnegative edge weights. Directed graphs need an explicit direction convention and normalization choice. Adding self-loops changes degrees and therefore all normalization weights, not only the diagonal entries. Expanded derivation Chapter source · PDF p. 24 Research reference Link to this calculation ↗ Equivariance versus invariance For node predictions, relabeling nodes should relabel outputs in the same way: permutation equivariance . For a single graph-level output, a symmetric readout such as summing final node embeddings produces permutation invariance . Those are different requirements. A graph classifier that changes prediction merely because rows were reordered violates the intended invariance. A node classifier must still preserve which output belongs to which node. Step by step Prove node equivariance and graph-level invariance Setting. Let node features be H and symmetrically normalized adjacency be S . A layer is F(H,A)=\sigma(SHW) with shared weights W and elementwise \sigma . Let P be a permutation matrix relabeling nodes. 1 · Relabel both features and relationships The relabeled features are H'=PH and adjacency A'=PAP^\top . Since PIP^\top=I , self-loop adjacency becomes \tilde A'=P\tilde AP^\top . Row sums reorder the degree entries, so \tilde D'=P\tilde DP^\top . 2 · Relabel normalization consistently For a positive diagonal degree matrix, taking inverse square roots reorders the same diagonal values: (\tilde D')^{-1/2}=P\tilde D^{-1/2}P^\top. Substituting into the normalized adjacency and canceling P^\top P=I gives S'=PSP^\top . 3 · Propagate and use shared elementwise operations F(H',A')=\sigma(S'H'W)=\sigma(PSP^\top PHW)=\sigma(PSHW). A row permutation commutes with the shared elementwise nonlinearity, so F(H',A')=P\sigma(SHW)=PF(H,A). Outputs reorder with nodes: equivariance. Permuting features without also permuting adjacency would describe a different graph and would not satisfy this calculation. 4 · Pool to get an invariant graph representation A sum readout is g=\mathbf1^\top H^{(L)} . Under relabeling, g'=\mathbf1^\top PH^{(L)}=\mathbf1^\top H^{(L)}=g, because \mathbf1^\top P=\mathbf1^\top . Mean and componentwise maximum pooling are also invariant to ordering. Shared edge scoring and permutation-symmetric aggregation preserve analogous properties in message-passing models. 5 · Keep symmetry distinct from expressiveness A model can obey the correct permutation symmetry and still fail to distinguish particular graph structures or long-range relationships. Equivariance is a consistency property under relabeling, not a universal expressiveness guarantee. Expanded derivation Chapter source · PDF p. 24 Research reference Link to this calculation ↗ Depth brings both reach and bottlenecks After L local message-passing layers without extra long-range edges, information can travel at most L graph hops. Repeated propagation can suppress discriminative node directions: over-smoothing . In a connected undirected graph, pure row-normalized diffusion approaches a common stationary average, whereas symmetric normalization approaches a degree-weighted dominant subspace. Raw node values need not all become equal; the expandable calculation below makes the distinction explicit. The source illustrates feature-variance loss under repeated graph diffusion. Real GNNs also include learned transforms and nonlinearities, so the plot isolates one mechanism. Architectures · PDF p. 26 Over-squashing is different: information from a rapidly growing distant neighborhood must pass through narrow graph bottlenecks into a fixed-width vector. Representations can remain distinct while still failing to convey enough distant information. The source also separates homophily—connected nodes being similar—from heterophily, where neighboring nodes can differ systematically. Naive averaging can be inappropriate when the relation means opposition, complementarity, or a different role rather than similarity. Step by step Derive the degree-weighted diffusion limit behind oversmoothing Setting. Consider repeated linear propagation on a connected undirected nonnegative graph with self-loops: H^{(L)}=S^LH^{(0)} , where S=\tilde D^{-1/2}\tilde A\tilde D^{-1/2} . Assume the associated random walk is irreducible and aperiodic, so the eigenvalue one is simple and all other eigenvalues have absolute value below one. 1 · Find the leading eigenvector Let v=\tilde D^{1/2}\mathbf1 , whose entries are \sqrt{\tilde d_i} . Then Sv=\tilde D^{-1/2}\tilde A\tilde D^{-1/2}\tilde D^{1/2}\mathbf1
=\tilde D^{-1/2}\tilde A\mathbf1
=\tilde D^{-1/2}\tilde D\mathbf1=v. Normalize it to u=v/\sqrt{\sum_i\tilde d_i} . 2 · Expand powers in an orthonormal eigenbasis Symmetry gives S=U\Lambda U^\top , with first column u and \lambda_1=1 . Thus S^L=uu^\top+\sum_{j=2}^n\lambda_j^L u_ju_j^\top. Because |\lambda_j|<1 for j\ge2 , each remaining power tends to zero. 3 · Write the limit explicitly H^{(L)}\longrightarrow uu^\top H^{(0)}. For one scalar feature, the limiting value at node i is h_i^{(\infty)}=\frac{\sqrt{\tilde d_i}}{\sum_j\tilde d_j}
\sum_j\sqrt{\tilde d_j}\,h_j^{(0)}. The result lies in a one-dimensional node subspace. Nodes need not have identical raw values when their degrees differ. 4 · Compare row-normalized diffusion For R=\tilde D^{-1}\tilde A , the limiting rows are identical stationary-distribution averages: R^L\longrightarrow\mathbf1\pi^\top,\qquad
\pi_i=\frac{\tilde d_i}{\sum_j\tilde d_j}. This is why “all nodes approach a common average” is literal for row-normalized connected aperiodic diffusion, but needs a degree-weighted qualification for symmetric normalization. 5 · Separate this mechanism from a full GNN theorem Learned transformations, nonlinearities, skip connections, disconnected components, and varying layer operators alter the dynamics. A raw feature-variance curve need not decrease monotonically under every such model. This simplified limit explains how repeated propagation can erase discriminative directions; over-squashing is a different limitation involving compression of many distant messages through narrow routes. The complete equations and worked values remain available in the calculation above. derivations.title: Calculate symmetric graph normalization, not just a neighbor mean
derivations.search:
**Setting.** Use an undirected three-node path $1\!-
obreakdash 2\!-
obreakdash 3$ with no initial self-loops. Each node has scalar feature $x=(2,1,4)^\top$. We will add one self-loop per node and use a scalar feature weight $w=0.5$ followed by ReLU.

#### 1 · Write adjacency and add self-loops
$$A=\begin{bmatrix}0&1&0\\1&0&1\\0&1&0\end{bmatrix},\qquad
\tilde A=A+I=\begin{bmatrix}1&1&0\\1&1&1\\0&1&1\end{bmatrix}.$$
Summing each row gives degrees $\tilde d=(2,3,2)$, so $\tilde D^{-1/2}=\operatorname{diag}(1/\sqrt2,1/\sqrt3,1/\sqrt2)$.

#### 2 · Multiply the diagonal factors into each edge
For $S=\tilde D^{-1/2}\tilde A\tilde D^{-1/2}$, entry $(i,j)$ is $\tilde A_{ij}/\sqrt{\tilde d_i\tilde d_j}$. Hence
$$S=\begin{bmatrix}
1/2&1/\sqrt6&0\\
1/\sqrt6&1/3&1/\sqrt6\\
0&1/\sqrt6&1/2
\end{bmatrix}.$$
This matrix is symmetric, but its rows do not generally sum to one.

#### 3 · Aggregate the features explicitly
$$m_1=\tfrac12(2)+\tfrac1{\sqrt6}(1)=1+\tfrac1{\sqrt6}\approx1.408248,$$
$$m_2=\tfrac1{\sqrt6}(2)+\tfrac13(1)+\tfrac1{\sqrt6}(4)
=\tfrac6{\sqrt6}+\tfrac13\approx2.782823,$$
$$m_3=\tfrac1{\sqrt6}(1)+\tfrac12(4)=\tfrac1{\sqrt6}+2\approx2.408248.$$
These are not the ordinary rowwise means $(1.5,7/3,2.5)$.

#### 4 · Apply the learned feature transformation and activation
$$h'=\operatorname{ReLU}(0.5m)\approx(0.704124,1.391412,1.204124)^\top.$$
All components are positive in this example. With multiple features, $H W$ transforms feature coordinates while $S$ mixes node coordinates; their roles differ.

#### 5 · State the graph assumptions
This symmetric construction has its usual spectral interpretation for an undirected graph with nonnegative edge weights. Directed graphs need an explicit direction convention and normalization choice. Adding self-loops changes degrees and therefore **all** normalization weights, not only the diagonal entries.

derivations.title: Prove node equivariance and graph-level invariance
derivations.search:
**Setting.** Let node features be $H$ and symmetrically normalized adjacency be $S$. A layer is $F(H,A)=\sigma(SHW)$ with shared weights $W$ and elementwise $\sigma$. Let $P$ be a permutation matrix relabeling nodes.

#### 1 · Relabel both features and relationships
The relabeled features are $H'=PH$ and adjacency $A'=PAP^\top$. Since $PIP^\top=I$, self-loop adjacency becomes $\tilde A'=P\tilde AP^\top$. Row sums reorder the degree entries, so $\tilde D'=P\tilde DP^\top$.

#### 2 · Relabel normalization consistently
For a positive diagonal degree matrix, taking inverse square roots reorders the same diagonal values:
$$(\tilde D')^{-1/2}=P\tilde D^{-1/2}P^\top.$$
Substituting into the normalized adjacency and canceling $P^\top P=I$ gives $S'=PSP^\top$.

#### 3 · Propagate and use shared elementwise operations
$$F(H',A')=\sigma(S'H'W)=\sigma(PSP^\top PHW)=\sigma(PSHW).$$
A row permutation commutes with the shared elementwise nonlinearity, so
$$F(H',A')=P\sigma(SHW)=PF(H,A).$$
Outputs reorder with nodes: equivariance. Permuting features without also permuting adjacency would describe a different graph and would not satisfy this calculation.

#### 4 · Pool to get an invariant graph representation
A sum readout is $g=\mathbf1^\top H^{(L)}$. Under relabeling,
$$g'=\mathbf1^\top PH^{(L)}=\mathbf1^\top H^{(L)}=g,$$
because $\mathbf1^\top P=\mathbf1^\top$. Mean and componentwise maximum pooling are also invariant to ordering. Shared edge scoring and permutation-symmetric aggregation preserve analogous properties in message-passing models.

#### 5 · Keep symmetry distinct from expressiveness
A model can obey the correct permutation symmetry and still fail to distinguish particular graph structures or long-range relationships. Equivariance is a consistency property under relabeling, not a universal expressiveness guarantee.

derivations.title: Derive the degree-weighted diffusion limit behind oversmoothing
derivations.search:
**Setting.** Consider repeated **linear** propagation on a connected undirected nonnegative graph with self-loops: $H^{(L)}=S^LH^{(0)}$, where $S=\tilde D^{-1/2}\tilde A\tilde D^{-1/2}$. Assume the associated random walk is irreducible and aperiodic, so the eigenvalue one is simple and all other eigenvalues have absolute value below one.

#### 1 · Find the leading eigenvector
Let $v=\tilde D^{1/2}\mathbf1$, whose entries are $\sqrt{\tilde d_i}$. Then
$$Sv=\tilde D^{-1/2}\tilde A\tilde D^{-1/2}\tilde D^{1/2}\mathbf1
=\tilde D^{-1/2}\tilde A\mathbf1
=\tilde D^{-1/2}\tilde D\mathbf1=v.$$
Normalize it to $u=v/\sqrt{\sum_i\tilde d_i}$.

#### 2 · Expand powers in an orthonormal eigenbasis
Symmetry gives $S=U\Lambda U^\top$, with first column $u$ and $\lambda_1=1$. Thus
$$S^L=uu^\top+\sum_{j=2}^n\lambda_j^L u_ju_j^\top.$$
Because $|\lambda_j|<1$ for $j\ge2$, each remaining power tends to zero.

#### 3 · Write the limit explicitly
$$H^{(L)}\longrightarrow uu^\top H^{(0)}.$$
For one scalar feature, the limiting value at node $i$ is
$$h_i^{(\infty)}=\frac{\sqrt{\tilde d_i}}{\sum_j\tilde d_j}
\sum_j\sqrt{\tilde d_j}\,h_j^{(0)}.$$
The result lies in a one-dimensional node subspace. Nodes need not have identical **raw** values when their degrees differ.

#### 4 · Compare row-normalized diffusion
For $R=\tilde D^{-1}\tilde A$, the limiting rows are identical stationary-distribution averages:
$$R^L\longrightarrow\mathbf1\pi^\top,\qquad
\pi_i=\frac{\tilde d_i}{\sum_j\tilde d_j}.$$
This is why “all nodes approach a common average” is literal for row-normalized connected aperiodic diffusion, but needs a degree-weighted qualification for symmetric normalization.

#### 5 · Separate this mechanism from a full GNN theorem
Learned transformations, nonlinearities, skip connections, disconnected components, and varying layer operators alter the dynamics. A raw feature-variance curve need not decrease monotonically under every such model. This simplified limit explains how repeated propagation can erase discriminative directions; over-squashing is a different limitation involving compression of many distant messages through narrow routes.

title: Reinforcement learning: rewards, values, and policies
summary: A compact bridge from prediction to sequential decisions: MDPs, Bellman equations, Q-learning and DQN, policy gradients, and PPO.
search:
An additional chapter based on official tutorials and primary RL references, not a chapter from the four original PDFs. The worked calculations are authored for this reader. Learning from consequences rather than labels A supervised learner is given target answers. A reinforcement-learning agent chooses an action, receives a reward and a new observation, and learns a policy for choosing future actions. An action can change not only the next reward but also which situations the agent encounters later. The central problem is therefore sequential decision-making , not predicting a supplied correct action. A robot can take a longer route to avoid a collision; a controller can accept a short-term cost to reach a more useful state. These are illustrative cases, not benchmarks. A neural network is optional: a small problem can use a table, while deep reinforcement learning uses neural networks to represent policies, value functions, or a model of the environment. A bandit is a useful simpler case where actions do not influence future decision states. In a fully observed Markov decision process (MDP) , the current state and action determine the distribution of the next state and reward; earlier history contributes no additional predictive information once they are known. An observation need not be a complete state. With partial observations, history, a belief state, or a recurrent representation may be needed—the connection to the RNN chapter . Quantity Meaning S_t=s State before decision t A_t=a Action taken at that decision R_{t+1} Reward produced by that action and transition p(s',r\mid s,a) Environment’s next-state and reward distribution \pi(a\mid s) Policy’s probability of choosing action a in state s \gamma Discount factor, which sets how future rewards enter the objective These definitions use R_{t+1} for the reward after A_t ; some tutorials call the same reward r_t . The indexing convention changes, not the interaction. Concepts and formalism ↗ Returns, values, and the Bellman equation For an episode with T actions, the return from decision t is G_t=\sum_{k=0}^{T-t-1}\gamma^kR_{t+k+1},\qquad G_T=0. This is a sum of rewards , not the immediate reward. With bounded rewards, 0\leq\gamma<1 also makes an infinite-horizon discounted return finite. A finite episode can use \gamma=1 . Discounting specifies the objective; it is not automatically a probability that the environment survives. The state value V^\pi(s)=\mathbb E_\pi[G_t\mid S_t=s] asks how good a state is under a particular policy . The action value Q^\pi(s,a)=\mathbb E_\pi[G_t\mid S_t=s,A_t=a] asks about taking one specified action and following that policy afterward. Hence V^\pi(s)=\sum_a\pi(a\mid s)Q^\pi(s,a). For a stationary discounted MDP, the Bellman expectation equation separates one reward from the remaining return: V^\pi(s)=\sum_a\pi(a\mid s)\sum_{s',r}p(s',r\mid s,a) igl[r+\gamma V^\pi(s') igr]. Terminal states have zero future value; the reward for entering them still counts. In a finite-horizon task, value can depend on remaining time, so use V_t^\pi or include time in the state. Averaging under \pi evaluates a policy. Replacing a future policy average by a maximum defines an optimality equation; it is a different operation. Value functions and Bellman equations ↗ Step by step From a discounted return to the Bellman equations Setting. An episode takes actions 0,\ldots,T-1 . Its final reward is R_T and G_T=0 . For the stationary Bellman form, use a stationary discounted MDP; for a finite-horizon example, include remaining time in the state. The following algebra is an authored expansion of the standard return and value definitions. 1 · Write out the discounted sum G_t=R_{t+1}+\gamma R_{t+2}+\gamma^2R_{t+3}+\cdots+\gamma^{T-t-1}R_T. The first reward has exponent zero because it is the next reward from the present decision. The next return begins one decision later: G_{t+1}=R_{t+2}+\gamma R_{t+3}+\cdots+\gamma^{T-t-2}R_T. 2 · Factor the common discount Every term after the first in G_t contains a factor \gamma . Factoring it leaves exactly G_{t+1} : G_t=R_{t+1}+\gamma igl[R_{t+2}+\gamma R_{t+3}+\cdots igr]=R_{t+1}+\gamma G_{t+1}. At the last decision this gives G_{T-1}=R_T+\gamma\cdot0=R_T . The same identity holds for a convergent infinite discounted sum. 3 · Condition on the present state By definition and linearity of conditional expectation, V^\pi(s)=\mathbb E_\pi[R_{t+1}+\gamma G_{t+1}\mid S_t=s]. First condition on the action, then on the next state and reward. The action has probability \pi(a\mid s) and the transition has probability p(s',r\mid s,a) . The Markov property and continuation under the same policy make the expected remaining return V^\pi(s') : V^\pi(s)=\sum_a\pi(a\mid s)\sum_{s',r}p(s',r\mid s,a) igl[r+\gamma V^\pi(s') igr]. These are sums for discrete states/rewards; continuous quantities require integrals. For a finite horizon without time in the state, replace the left value by V_t^\pi(s) and the continuation by V_{t+1}^\pi(s') . 4 · Hold the first action fixed If the first action is specified rather than sampled, remove the first policy average: Q^\pi(s,a)=\sum_{s',r}p(s',r\mid s,a) igl[r+\gamma V^\pi(s') igr]. The maximum stays inside the next-state expectation because the next action is chosen after observing the next state. It is not a maximum over the environment’s random outcomes. 5 · Work backward through a small choice At s_0 , either collect reward 2 and stop, or wait through rewards (0,0,4) before stopping. A policy that waits half the time has expected return 2.620. The optimal choice is wait. Temporal-difference (TD) learning uses an estimated future value to construct a target immediately; this is called bootstrapping . Here, bootstrapping is not the resampling procedure in the bagging chapter. For estimating the value of the policy generating the data, TD(0) uses \delta_t=R_{t+1}+\gamma(1-d_t)V(S_{t+1})-V(S_t), V(S_t)\leftarrow V(S_t)+\alpha\delta_t. The original PPO paper gives the algorithmic rationale. Practical checks before trusting a result Termination is not truncation. A true terminal state has no continuation value. An artificial rollout/time cutoff in an otherwise continuing task normally still needs bootstrapping from the final observation. End the collection episode on terminated or truncated , but suppress the bootstrap on terminated . A genuine finite task horizon is part of the state/task definition. Never bootstrap from the next episode’s reset observation. Gymnasium’s worked explanation ↗ Evaluate the behavior, not only the surrogate loss. Check held-out rollouts, multiple random seeds, episode returns, failure rates, and environment interactions used. A low TD or actor loss does not by itself mean a useful policy. Keep evaluation settings explicit, including whether actions are sampled or chosen deterministically. A reward is a proxy for the task: maximizing it can exploit a simulator shortcut or an unintended incentive. Evaluation and debugging guidance ↗ This is a foundations supplement, not a complete treatment of continuous-control algorithms, offline RL, model-based planning, or reinforcement learning from human feedback.
