derivations.title: From a discounted return to the Bellman equations
derivations.search: Step by step From a discounted return to the Bellman equations Setting. An episode takes actions 0,\ldots,T-1 . Its final reward is R_T and G_T=0 . For the stationary Bellman form, use a stationary discounted MDP; for a finite-horizon example, include remaining time in the state. The following algebra is an authored expansion of the standard return and value definitions. 1 · Write out the discounted sum G_t=R_{t+1}+\gamma R_{t+2}+\gamma^2R_{t+3}+\cdots+\gamma^{T-t-1}R_T. The first reward has exponent zero because it is the next reward from the present decision. The next return begins one decision later: G_{t+1}=R_{t+2}+\gamma R_{t+3}+\cdots+\gamma^{T-t-2}R_T. 2 · Factor the common discount Every term after the first in G_t contains a factor \gamma . Factoring it leaves exactly G_{t+1} : G_t=R_{t+1}+\gamma\bigl[R_{t+2}+\gamma R_{t+3}+\cdots\bigr]=R_{t+1}+\gamma G_{t+1}. At the last decision this gives G_{T-1}=R_T+\gamma\cdot0=R_T . The same identity holds for a convergent infinite discounted sum. 3 · Condition on the present state By definition and linearity of conditional expectation, V^\pi(s)=\mathbb E_\pi[R_{t+1}+\gamma G_{t+1}\mid S_t=s]. First condition on the action, then on the next state and reward. The action has probability \pi(a\mid s) and the transition has probability p(s',r\mid s,a) . The Markov property and continuation under the same policy make the expected remaining return V^\pi(s') : V^\pi(s)=\sum_a\pi(a\mid s)\sum_{s',r}p(s',r\mid s,a)\bigl[r+\gamma V^\pi(s')\bigr]. These are sums for discrete states/rewards; continuous quantities require integrals. For a finite horizon without time in the state, replace the left value by V_t^\pi(s) and the continuation by V_{t+1}^\pi(s') . 4 · Hold the first action fixed If the first action is specified rather than sampled, remove the first policy average: Q^\pi(s,a)=\sum_{s',r}p(s',r\mid s,a)\bigl[r+\gamma V^\pi(s')\bigr]. Under an optimal policy, the best next-state value is \max_{a'}Q^*(s',a') , giving Q^*(s,a)=\sum_{s',r}p(s',r\mid s,a)\bigl[r+\gamma\max_{a'}Q^*(s',a')\bigr]. The maximum stays inside the next-state expectation because the next action is chosen after observing the next state. It is not a maximum over the environment’s random outcomes. 5 · Work backward through a small choice At s_0 , either collect reward 2 and stop, or wait through rewards (0,0,4) before stopping. After choosing to wait, the two remaining actions are forced. With \gamma=0.9 , V(s_2)=4,\qquad V(s_1)=0+0.9(4)=3.6, Q(s_0,\mathrm{wait})=0+0.9(3.6)=3.24,\qquad Q(s_0,\mathrm{stop})=2. If the policy waits with probability p=0.5 , its starting value is V^\pi(s_0)=(1-p)2+p(4\gamma^2)=0.5(2)+0.5(3.24)=2.62. The optimal action is wait when 4\gamma^2>2 , so the threshold is \gamma>\sqrt{1/2}\approx0.7071 . Changing \gamma changes the preference even though neither path’s actual rewards change. Take 2 now, or 4 two steps later? Reset Discount γ 0.90 Probability of waiting 0.50 Stop now 2.000 Wait 3.240 Policy value 2.620 At γ = 0.90, waiting returns 3.240. A policy that waits half the time has expected return 2.620. The optimal choice is wait. derivations.title: A Q-learning target and update, one calculation at a time
derivations.search: Step by step A Q-learning target and update, one calculation at a time Setting. One observed transition is (s,a,r,s',d) , where d records genuine termination. Use a scalar table entry q=Q(s,a) and hold the target fixed during this update. This calculation describes a tabular Q-learning step and then its neural-network analogue; it is not a convergence proof. 1 · Form the continuation target For a nonterminal transition, choose the largest estimated next-action value, then discount it and add the observed reward: y=r+\gamma(1-d)\max_{a'}Q(s',a'). When d=1 , the future term vanishes but the immediate reward remains. A sampled target is not the same as the exact Bellman expectation. 2 · Measure the prediction error Define \delta=y-q . A positive \delta means the target is above the current estimate. Use a half-squared loss to make the derivative simple: \ell(q)=\tfrac12(q-y)^2. 3 · Differentiate and take a descent step The derivative of the square is twice its argument. The inner derivative is 1 because y is fixed: \frac{d\ell}{dq}=\tfrac12\cdot2(q-y)\cdot1=q-y=-\delta. Gradient descent subtracts this derivative: q_{\mathrm{new}}=q-\alpha(q-y)=q+\alpha\delta=(1-\alpha)q+\alpha y. For 0\leq\alpha\leq1 , this is a weighted average of the old estimate and the target. 4 · Substitute actual values Let q=1.5 , r=1 , \gamma=0.9 , \max_{a'}Q(s',a')=3 , d=0 , and \alpha=0.2 : y=1+0.9(3)=3.7,\qquad\delta=3.7-1.5=2.2, q_{\mathrm{new}}=1.5+0.2(2.2)=1.94. For the otherwise identical terminal transition, y=1 and q_{\mathrm{new}}=1.5+0.2(1-1.5)=1.4 . Confusing an artificial time cutoff with termination would therefore change the target and update. 5 · Replace the table entry with a network prediction For network parameters \theta , the chain rule gives \nabla_\theta\ell=\bigl(Q_\theta(s,a)-y\bigr)\nabla_\theta Q_\theta(s,a). A target network Q_{\bar\theta} forms y with fixed parameters and disabled gradient tracking. The shared network update can change many state-action predictions at once, unlike updating one table entry. DQN often replaces the squared loss with Huber/Smooth L1 loss to limit the influence of large residuals. The official tutorial shows that implementation explicitly.
